speakeroldname: Hon. Bill McKnight (Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development):
speakerposition: Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development
subsubtopic: NATIVE LAND CLAIMS POLICY-STATEMENT BY MINISTER
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, today I have the pleasure to announce the culmination of one of the critical initiatives undertaken by my Ministry-a comprehensive native land claims policy. I believe it represents yet another milestone in the evolving relationship between the Government and Canada's native people.
From the beginning of our mandate we recognized the vital role which Canada's native people play. Our commitment to the establishment of a relationship built upon mutual trust and confidence remains strong. Our achievements over the past 2.5 years have been many.
We live in a period of great hope for the future of the country, and I feel that our original inhabitants must play a key role in shaping it. After all, it is in the interest of all Canadians to search for and to find an amicable arrangement whereby both native and non-native communities can agree on how we will live together in Canada.
Upon assuming office the Government was faced with a comprehensive land claims policy which was out of touch. If anything, it raised obstacles to settlements rather than contributing to them. Native people were calling for change in much the same way as Canadians had voted for change. We
listened, we consulted, and today we are delivering. Now, more than ever before, we have an opportunity to complete the modern claims process in Canada through a more flexible, realistic, and responsive comprehensive land claims policy.
It has not been an easy task, and it has taken us longer to put it in place than anyone ever imagined. Still, it has been a valuable learning experience for all. It has certainly been a learning experience for me in the short six months I have spent in this office.
I am sure my predecessor, the Hon. Member for Rosedale (Mr. Crombie), would agree with that statement. After all, he started the ball rolling with the appointment of a federal task force to review the whole area of comprehensive claims. At that time the Minister was convinced that the report of the task force, headed by the very capable Murray Coolican, would provide the informed, thoughtful, and independent appraisal and recommendations we have needed for some time. The Hon. Member has certainly lived up to that billing.
Over the past several months while the report was being given a public airing, we have continued to receive innumerable representations from native groups. Frankly, I have been impressed with the importance which native leaders, the provinces, the territories, and other interested Canadians have placed on the matter. In particular I should like to pay tribute to the worth-while contribution made by the Comprehensive Claims Coalition, chaired by Joanne Barnaby. This group participated in the formulation of the policy in a reasoned and reasonable way.
In the few minutes I have, I should like to outline some of the major elements of the comprehensive native land claims policy. Today I issued a policy paper and other supporting documents which explain it in more detail. First, I affirm the Government's commitment to settling comprehensive claims through negotiations on a basis which is equitable to native people and other Canadians. Also I want to announce that the federal Government stands ready to consider two alternatives to the extinguishment of aboriginal rights through claims settlements while still obtaining certainty of rights and title to the use of lands. As we all know, the language of extinguishment has long been a concern to many native people. Any other aboriginal rights which may exist will remain unaffected by comprehensive claims agreements.
A new feature of the claims policy is the provision for the enhancement of economic development and self-government- two of the Government's cornerstones in its relationship with native people. I am pleased to announce that the policy will allow for the negotiation of a broader range of self-government

December 18, 1986
Statements by Ministers
matters. The negotiations will be consistent with the Government's policy on community based Indian and Inuit selfgovernment, will respect existing constitutional principles and government practice, and will take into account any directions north of 60 toward public Government and devolution.
As we all know, the test for any self-government arrangement is its appropriateness in meeting the needs of native communities and its capacity to enhance the quality of life of individual members of the communities. I believe the policy provides for that.
The policy also contains important provisions aimed at enhancing native decision making in the area of natural resources. In this regard it is expected that settlements will recognize a particular aboriginal managerial interest in relation to environmental matters including land use, water, and wildlife.
It is particularly important to note that the federal Government stands ready to negotiate matters related to the harvesting and management of renewable resources with aboriginal groups which have made traditional use of coastal and other marine areas.
In addition, under the new policy, the federal Government is prepared to assign to aboriginal groups a percentage of the Crown's royalties derived from the extraction of resources in the entire settlement area. I should add that this option will include not only the royalties from subsurface resources, but also from non-renewable resources extracted from offshore areas that form part of the claims settlement area. In addition, we will be instituting a number of important principles and processes aimed at ensuring the more expeditious negotiation and settlement of claims. We stand on the threshold of what I hope to be many comprehensive claims settlements in the coming years, more living treaties and lasting agreements. We have the tools; all that is required is the good will and cooperation of all parties.
Many months ago, the Hon. Member for Rosedale laid the cornerstones for the Government's aboriginal policies and cemented a new and growing relationship with native people. It is upon this foundation-Indian self-government, economic development, quality of community life, and the protection of the special relationship between the federal Government and Indian people-that my colleagues and I have continued to build. My sincere hope is that we can continue travelling down this road together. I hope all Members of this House will support this policy initiative as it affects native people and all Canadians.

subsubtopic: NATIVE LAND CLAIMS POLICY-STATEMENT BY MINISTER
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I want to begin by commending both the Minister and his predecessor for recognizing the urgent need for a new comprehensive claims policy. It was called for by the Special Committee on Indian Self-government in Canada, as the Minister mentioned. It has long been demanded by the claimant groups.
It is self-evident that we need a new claims policy because so few claims have been settled. That is the case and it is to our shame.
There is a growing insistence by the territorial Governments, by those who advocate aboriginal rights, and by those who wish to proceed with developmental plans on aboriginal lands, that settlements be made and that they be made as soon as possible. I say that the guiding light for a new comprehensive claims policy certainly lies with that excellent report by Mr. Murray Coolican, known as the Coolican Report. What the Minister has announced today as a new comprehensive claims policy is not precisely, fully and exactly as contained in the Coolican Report. It is, I submit, a careful, cautious and modest step from what we had before. In other words, I acknowledge to the Minister and the House that the new comprehensive claims policy is an improvement on the past. It is progressive and a step forward.
However, the difficulty with the new claims policy, as with the old, is that it stems from a premise narrow in scope and fragile in structure, that is, that aboriginal title involves traditional use and occupancy which continues in certain respects up to the present. This so-called title as the Government sees it is an annoyance. It is a thorn in its side which must somehow be removed so that the Government of Canada can get on with its dealings and arrangements with third parties in order to advance and enhance what it describes as the public interest. I wish to assert to the House and the Minister that the premise which underlies aboriginal title is neither narrow in scope nor fragile in construction. It is broadly based and very firm and strong.
What is really in question in Canada today, what is in doubt, is the Crown's right. Where aboriginal title is being asserted and where there is no treaty or agreement in existence, there, Sir, the Crown right is in doubt. I therefore argue that the impetus to settle rests much more with the Government than with any claimant group. For us to define aboriginal title in its narrowest terms, I say to this Government as I said to the previous Government, is both arrogant and presumptuous. Some argue that aboriginal title is limited or confined only to traditional pursuits, hunting, fishing and trapping. Even in those areas Governments always seek ways to limit and control. Now, with this new policy, I suspect the attitude remains very much the same as in the past. The difference is that the Government is saying to the aboriginal claimant groups that it is prepared to be a little more generous, a little more open-handed than Governments in the past. For example, the new claims policy says that the federal Government is prepared to assign a percentage of Crown royalties from extraction of resources in the entire settlement area. I say to the Government that aboriginal title is all inclusive, not exclusive. It is not limited to traditional pursuits based solely on use and occupancy in the past. A sharing of revenues from resource development is not largesse or generosity by the Government or people of Canada. It must be part and parcel of an agreement reached through negotiation.
December 18, 1986

I therefore turn my attention to third parties and the public interest. They both fall squarely under the umbrella of Crown right and they have yet to be defined and determined. They are not at this moment, as the new policy states, legitimate. They are still indeterminate and must be clearly defined. To sum up, it is not the Government's right to determine just how benevolent it is prepared to be in the settlement of aboriginal claims. The Crown's right is in question and in doubt. It is up to the claimant groups, as much as it is up to the Government, to determine just how generous they will be with us.
I submit that all the high cards are not in our hands. The Government says it prefers negotiations to litigation. No wonder. I believe there is an underlying fear, suspicion and concern that the case for aboriginal title is exceedingly strong and if we proceed to litigation we may learn that fact in ways unacceptable to the Government of Canada. I say to the Minister that I, too, prefer negotiation, but I say to the Government: Stop pretending that you are the big guy on the block because you are not.
I turn very briefly to the question of self-government which is referred to on page nine of the policy. At first glance it seems there is a willingness on the part of the Government to negotiate aboriginal self-government within the agreement. However, I see a lure on this fish-hook. It is this. The Minister says to the aboriginal claimant groups, "Do not let yourselves become beguiled into thinking that self-government provisions are going to become constitutionally entrenched." That will not happen, he says. He is thus declaring that there will be no bottom up approach to aboriginal self-government being entrenched in the Constitution of Canada. The Constitution now allows for that to happen. The Minister says it will not happen. He is saying to the provinces that they will continue to have a very big voice and that we will only proceed by way of the top down approach. I think that has to be looked at and challenged another time.
There are other matters I wish to raise with the Minister, Sir, but you are signalling that my time is up. I just want to say that the Minister must do more to protect implementation, and on another occasion, in another forum, I will elaborate on that. In conclusion, there is goodwill and co-operation on this side of the House. We, too, want these negotiations to be settled in an equitable, fair and just way for the aboriginal claimant groups of the country.

subsubtopic: NATIVE LAND CLAIMS POLICY-STATEMENT BY MINISTER
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is my pleasure to rise and declare the broad agreement of my Party with the principle of the comprehensive land claims policy tabled by the Minister in Parliament this morning. At the same time, I must also state a profound dissatisfaction with what I see as the vagueness and inadequacy of the Minister's statement.
It is one year since the Coolican Report was presented to the Minister's predecessor. One year is surely too long for the production of such a document as we have seen today. It is
Statements by Ministers
surely too long for the sort of vague, over-all endorsement of the Coolican Report which the Minister's statement has provided. After one year the Government has at least acknowledged favourably the four main principles of the Coolican Report, those being that self-government is a major concern of the Indian and Inuit people in the claims areas, that the rights of aboriginal people should not be extinguished, that there should be aboriginal participation in resource management, and that there must be a benefit from the royalties derived from the exploitation of non-renewable resources.
Unfortunately, many aboriginal people will be somewhat disappointed and disturbed by the apparent overcoming of the concerns of the Coolican Report by the legal reservations of the Department of Justice through the framing of terminology. Nevertheless, I believe that the two alternatives given provide adequate recognition of the desire of aboriginal people not to see the formal and final extinguishment of their aboriginal rights. The Minister has clearly recognized the right of aboriginal people to stewardship over the resources of which they are and will continue to be until the time of a settlement the true owners and inheritors.
A commitment has been made in this presentation. However, it will be judged by the keeping rather than the pledging. I believe that we have seen today the removal of obstacles to the Dene, CYI and TFN claims. I am glad that by recognizing that a royalty right exists for the whole area rather than simply the retained lands, we will at last have a refutation of the maxim of John Paul Getty that the meek shall inherit the earth, but not the mineral rights thereof.
The language of the assignment of these rights is unfortunate. The language in which self-government is discussed is also unfortunate. I believe that self-government is entrenched in the Cree Naskapi Act. If that is in place for those communities, why not for the communities which will be affected by this policy?
I know that the Minister does not believe that all problems will be solved by this policy. I am glad that he has frankly acknowledged the problems of convincing the Government of British Columbia to deal fairly and realistically with the native people of that province, recognizing history and jurisprudence. The time strictures given in the policy remain to be proven. The lack of a detailed policy manual and an individual mandate for federal negotiators indicates that we have today seen only the first third of this process. The negotiation process will not be judged by what is said here today, but rather by what is done, by history. I, therefore, charge the Government to examine the record with regard to the James Bay Treaty, the Cree Naskapi Act, and to ensure that some of the problems encountered there are not encountered with settlements to be made under this new policy.
Unfortunately, there was no statement on the expansion of the short list of six claims to be negotiated at one time. There is no new commitment by the Government on the funding and resourcing of negotiations. This calls into question the negotiating process because, above all, the people of Canada

December 18, 1986
Committee Reports
and the world must see that these are genuine negotiations between nations, albeit one large and one small, which both parties are able to treat as such.
Our Party is broadly satisfied to have this policy tabled, although the criticism I have made must stand. I do not agree with the Member for Cochrane-Superior (Mr. Penner) that the Government has taken a step forward, but I do acknowledge that it has at least freed its shoes. We look to the Government to take steps forward in the future. I assure the Minister and his colleagues that we will be behind them, pushing.

subsubtopic: PUBLIC ACCOUNTS-SECOND REPORT OF STANDING COMMITTEE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have the honour to present the second report of the Public Accounts Committee. In the April, 1985, report to the House, the committee was concerned about the failure of Treasury Board to enforce its rules and the failure of the Department of Public Works to follow them. We are still concerned with this problem. It seems to us that reasonable rules from the Treasury Board should be followed. If the rules are too rigid or out of date, then that problem should be addressed. However, we cannot see that the interests of the taxpayers are well served by having rules on paper which are ignored. This applies to, among other things, cost overruns and contractsplitting. There is a continuing problem with respect to those which needs to be addressed.
We also see a need to improve communications because client Departments do not seem to be fully aware of the cost implications of making changes after a building program has begun. We think it is important for the Department of Public Works to ensure that requirements are clearly defined before contracts or projects are approved. The committee strongly disapproves of situations such as contract-splitting where the Department of Public Works knew in advance that Treasury Board approval would be required but did not seek it.

speechtext:
That Supplementary Estimates (B) for the fiscal year ending March 31, 1987, laid upon the Table Wednesday, December 17, 1986, be concurred in.

December 18, 1986
Supplementary Estimates (B), 1986-87
He said: Mr. Speaker, I am appearing before the House today to seek approval of the Supplementary Estimates for the first payment under the Special Canadian Grains Program. The need for this program is clear. Canadian grain and oil seed farmers are suffering the effects of extremely low world grain prices. Low prices stem from an international subsidy war. Massive subsidies and surpluses of grain have built up in most food producing countries.
The United States and the European Economic Community are attempting to sell off their surpluses by using huge export subsidies. These unfair practices have pushed grain prices to their lowest level in real terms in about 50 years. Canada is taking advantage of every possible opportunity to restore fairness and sanity to international agricultural trade. We have made some progress, but it will be a long and difficult task.
In the meantime our grain and oil seed farmers need extra help. The stakes of the subsidy war are very high. They are too high for most other countries, including Canada, to compete. However, within our fiscal means we are coming to the aid of Canadian farmers.
Although we have introduced many special measures, including the fuel tax rebate, interest rate rebate, and the freezing of freight rates, just to name a few, we also announced on December 9 the details of the Special Canadian Grains Program which is a $1 billion program aimed at helping Canadian grain and oil seeds farmers. This assistance will cushion the impact on our farmers of the global subsidy trade war.
I ask Hon. Members to remember that it is the crop year, not the fiscal year or calendar year that is important to farmers. I have given my commitment that the full benefits of the program will be in the hands and pockets of Canadian farmers by next spring.
Today I am seeking the approval of the Supplementary Estimates covering the first payment to farmers under this program. These estimates are split into two votes; the first amount of $296,015 million is a vote under grants and contributions. Another $3,985 million will cover the administrative costs. I am sure Hon. Members will appreciate that this is a program of considerable, in fact, historic magnitude and we want the program administered properly, accurately and well.
The administrative costs include staff salaries, supplies, computer services, equipment rentals, printing and mailing costs and public information measures to ensure that farmers are aware of their entitlement and eligibility and are aware of the March 31 deadline for applications. I am seeking approval before Christmas rather than after because I want the benefits to reach farmers just as soon as possible. The speedy approval of these Estimates by the House will allow the federal Government to disburse the money to farmers beginning next
month. If we were to wait until after Christmas, disbursement of the funds could not begin until well into February.
I am sure that all Hon. Members of the House would agree that farmers need cash flow help now. I, therefore, ask for their co-operation in approving these Estimates as quickly as possible in the interests and benefit of Canadian farmers across this country.
Hear, hear!

Mr. Speaker, we are pleased that the Minister has brought forward the Supplementary Estimates for at least part of the payments to be made under the Special Canadian Grains Program. The initial payment is some $300 million. We wish the Minister had brought forward the full $1 billion at this time because the money is urgently needed by Canada's grain producers in all parts of the country.
We will have a number of questions to ask when the Bill comes before the House and we are in Committee of the Whole. I was surprised that the Minister mentioned things such as the freezing of freight rates and the fuel tax rebate because he knows, of course, that the freezing of the freight rates was not really a freezing but an order by his Government to recalculate the volumes of grain to be shipped. Therefore, there is really no freezing, but just a recalculation.
Interestingly enough, the decision by the Government to order the grain transportation agencies to reduce the volumes will come back to haunt the Government because it is going to have to raise freight rates in the upcoming crop year partly because the Government ordered the Department of Transport to recalculate those volumes.
When the Minister spoke about the fuel tax rebate being cut back, he did not mention that a year ago the Government imposed a two cents per litre fuel tax on farmers, and that after being hammered by the Opposition and by farmers all last winter, the Government last May took that fuel tax off. I was surprised, therefore, that the Minister mentioned those items.
Although we are very pleased to see the Estimates come before the House, we are surprised there is no schedule showing where the funds are coming from to assist Canadian farmers. We assume the funds do not come from essential services to all Canadians. We would propose, if the Minister would only listen to us, that perhaps he table in the House today or tomorrow something to show exactly where the funds are coming from, so that in giving our unanimous support to pass these Estimates and the legislation today, we will know that the funds are not coming from essential services for all Canadians. We are certainly very insistent they do not.
The Minister talked about the trade war going on between the EEC and the United States. In fact, farmers are facing the worst financial crisis since the 1930s. Grain prices are the lowest in real terms since that time. In the last two years since this Government has come to power, the asset value of Canadian farm operations, according to a calculation by the
December 18, 1986

Farm Credit Corporation, has dropped by some 19 per cent. That represents some $20 billion. If the situation continues to be as bad over the next two years as it has been over the first two years of this administration, it will mean a drop in farm asset value of some $40 billion, which will reduce it from about $115 billion, as it was in 1984, to about $75 billion. That would certainly be the most serious decline in farm asset value in the history of our country, certainly since the Great Depression of the 1930s. We will be interested when we are in Committee of the Whole to know exactly how the Government plans to cope with this monumental decrease in value. For a farmer who has 100 per cent equity in his farm, the loss of equity is not as serious as it is for those young farmers who have high debts because, of course, the loss of that asset value comes out of their equity. Literally thousands of farmers have lost their farms during the last two years because of that dramatic drop in asset and equity value.
I hope the Minister will be able to explain why he is not delaying the lifting of the Farm Credit Corporation moratorium on farm foreclosures until the final payment is made under the Special Canadian Grains Program. If the Government can delay the final payment under this Special Canadian Grains Program for two, three, four or five months, surely it can postpone the lifting of the moratorium on farm foreclosures.
It is clear to all Canadians that the Government has done extremely little for the farm debt crisis. In fact, only one program, the commodity based mortgage program, which is providing some $20 million of interest assistance this year, is provided for the farm debt crisis, and that is a paltry amount when compared to the thousands of farmers who are losing their farms.
Groups like the United Grain Growers have estimated that it would take $4 billion in deficiency payments to put the Canadian farmer on an equal footing with the United States farmer. Groups like the pool elevator groups in the Prairies have called for the Government to pay at least $2 billion or $3 billion. Therefore, the amount being offered by the Government for this program is extremely small compared to the amount in those Estimates.
I would hope that when we are in Committee of the Whole, the Minister will be able to clarify a number of other items. I do not see any provision in the Estimates to ensure that the money received by prairie farmers, which I understand is about 85 per cent, will not be counted in the calculations of the Western Grain Stabilization Fund. I hope the Minister will be able to explain that. Perhaps it is in the Bill which will be introduced, but it is not clear in the Estimates.
The average payment under this program is some $5,000. The average initial payment, therefore, at 30 per cent, is $1,500. I hope that the Minister will be able to explain how such a small payment in January or February will prevent literally thousands of farmers who are facing serious financial difficulty from entering into foreclosure situations.
Supplementary Estimates (B), 1986-87
The association which represents Ontario soybean producers has pointed out that the assistance it is receiving under this program gives it something in the order of 92 per cent of the average assistance from this program and under the Agricultural Stabilization Act, whereas all other producers in Ontario are receiving approximately 100 per cent of the last five years' average. I hope that issue will be something the government committee which is to be established will be able to rectify since there will be an eastern and a western committee to review such problems.
I wish to indicate our support for the concurrence motion in the Estimates with the caveats I have outlined.

Mr. Speaker,
I wish to make a few brief comments about the proposal which is now before us which, essentially, will provide some $300 million of the $1 billion aid package to western farmers. In the Supplemenary Estimates which have been put before us, the program is called "Special Canadian Grains Program, 1986 Crop". Since this debate began, part of the Bill that goes with the Supplementary Estimates has been circulated. I would like to point out that it is not clear whether the $1 billion, when it does receive final approval by the House and is in the hands of farmers, will be treated as something separate from grains income. The fact that the Government has chosen to call it a grains program will require the Minister to provide an explanation when we come to consideration of this matter in Committee of the Whole in the event that future Governments may decide that this aid was in fact grain income which, therefore, will result in a reduction. It would be a fairly major reduction in the pay-outs to be made under the Western Grain Stabilization Act or under the Agricultural Stabilization Act in eastern Canada. So we will be asking the Minister some questions in this respect when the time comes.
Even after the $1 billion has been paid out I think we should realize that 1986 has not been a banner year for farmers. The Outlook Conference which took place in Ottawa a short while ago showed that the expected net income for farmers in 1986 will be $3.8 billion, which is an increase of 18 per cent. The fact that it is said that this is an increase of 18 per cent sounds as if farmers were doing fairly well. However, when we take this figure of $3.8 billion and put it in a historical context we realize that in 1974, just 12 years ago, farmers had a net income of just over $3.5 billion. This was at a time when the dollar bought much more than twice of what it buys in 1986. Only then can we begin to comprehend what has actually happened to net farm income.
While I am on my feet I would like to make the following explanation. I realize that members of the business press never listen to speeches on agriculture which, perhaps, explains why they report agricultural issues so poorly. However, for the benefit of those few Members who are in the House today I will make a brief explanation in the hope that they will realize when they read the press reports what the error implies. I read

reports in The Globe and Mail with respect to the recent Outlook Conference at which farmers' incomes for the coming year were plotted out. One such article appeared in the business section of The Globe and Mail where one would think one would find reasonably accurate reportage. The article covers three types of farmers and shows what the coming year holds in store for them. An Alberta cow-calf operator, an Ontario mixed farmer and a typical Saskatchewan grain farmer are the three examples considered in the article. It is pointed out, for instance, that the Alberta cow-calf rancher will have a fairly good year. This fairly large ranch in Alberta will have a realized net income of $26,000. I take issue with the reporter who states that "realized net income" is code for profit. No way, Mr. Speaker. It is not code for profit.
Realized net income is net income, the amount of income that is left over to pay a managerial income to the farmer or rancher and some return on his or her investment. A net income of $26,000 on the cow-calf operation being considered here would not even cover a decent return on investment. It is not profit. It barely brings this rancher up to the average industrial wage. If we were to give him an average industrial wage, that would leave him with less than $6,000 as a return on his investment, which was probably in excess of $500,000. I wish that some of the business reporters in the country would realize what the term "realized net income" means. It means only the money that is left over after all of the expenses have been paid. It is the pool of money which pays the operator and his family their wages. It pays them for whatever fee they might have coming to them for management and it also pays them for their investment. It is a conglomeration of what private corporations would have under three headings. If this particular cow-calf operator in Alberta used corporate accounting methods, he would probably show a net loss much in excess of the $26,000 that The Globe and Mail reporter calls net profit.
I wanted to make this point because when people are reporting about this $1 billion they ought to have the right figures before they start talking about it. I think it is understood by most agricultural economists and farm managers that the $1 billion pay-out will not come out as $1 billion of net profit. A big chunk of it will go to pay off existing debts and costs that have been left unpaid and will therefore not reflect straight through the system as an additional $1 billion of net income. I think it is fairly clear that this $1 billion is an attempt to make adjustments for the hurt that has affected Canada's grain farmers as a result of the U.S. Farm Bill. This hurt has been estimated accurately by a number of groups, ranging from the United Grain Growers Limited to the Ontario Institute of Agrologists to the Saskatchewan Wheat Pool and other groups, including the National Farmers Union and the federations of agriculture, to be somewhere in the area of just over $4 billion. The U.S. Farm Bill and the war that has broken out between the Europeans and the Americans has caused Canada's agricultural community and its grain producers more than $4 billion in hurt. The Government is
now attempting to ease that burden by a quarter. While it is appreciated, it does not take away the hurt.

Canadians should realize that net incomes for Saskatchewan farmers will be down considerably this year as will net incomes for farmers from other prairie provinces where grains are produced. Net incomes in Saskatchewan are predicted to be down by 27 per cent. For Manitoba, the figure is 51 per cent and for Alberta 64 per cent. These figures speak of a year that uses as its base a year that was almost a disaster. The fact that income is dropping by half is not telling all of the story. Incomes are dropping from levels that were not up to 1974-75 levels. The industry has been in difficulty for three to five years and net incomes have not been up to par for that time. We in the farming community will have to learn to accept further cut-backs even with this injection of an additional $1 billion.
We want to make certain that Canadian taxpayers who are being asked to pick up the tab for this assistance will realize just how bad the situation is. Because the Government wishes to press other business through the House in the next couple of days, I will not take too much more of the time of the House explaining the great contribution agriculture makes to the Canadian economy. I would hope that this is understood, but I realize that it is not something that is well understood by Canadians. It is not understood that agriculture is still the backbone of Canada's economy in most parts of the country and that keeping farmers on the land is important in maintaining communities and smaller cities that depend almost entirely on agricultural output.
With this $300 million which will come in this fiscal year because we are deeming the Bill to have been passed by Parliament on April 1, 1986, some nine months ago, we will attempt to pick up some of this shortfall in the marketing system. It will be an attempt to help with the inability of Canada and other exporters to bring the American and European trade war to heel.

I will start with the Hon. Member's first question. The moneys received under this program will not be counted as income for the purpose of the calculation of the western grain stabilization payments.
I have answered the question regarding fiscal framework on a number of occasions. As the Hon. Member will know,
because of the priority that we place on agriculture and because that industry is having the toughest time for 50 years, we have had to respond with millions and millions of dollars. On each and every occasion we have responded to the need, and each and every occasion has been within the fiscal framework.
The Hon. Member asks when the cheques will be in the hands of Canadian farmers. With his co-operation today, it will allow us to place cheques in the pockets of the Canadian farmers who are permit book holders in western Canada because we have that accurate up-to-date information. I was assured by officials that we have booked a slot with DSS and these cheques should be sent from Ottawa about the middle of next month.
On those farmers in eastern Canada who received ASA payments for corn, soybeans, and so on, we do have that information. At least, we have their names, addresses, and postal codes. Therefore, that will allow us to forward application forms immediately. They will be in a position to receive cheques at the next earliest date.
The only way that those farmers in eastern Canada and western Canada who do not fall into those categories can be reached is through the depositing of application forms in FCC offices, in grain offices, and in grain elevator offices across the country.
The March 31 deadline is a very important deadline. By at that time we will want to have received all of the information for the final payment. It is important that farmers be aware of that March 31 deadline in order that the information in all of the categories, commodities and grains that qualify across the country are in our hands so that we can do the final calculation with respect to an update on the hurt factor.
The delivery time of the final payment will largely depend on the farmers' ability to respond promptly and accurately. As the Hon. Member will know, oftentimes the issuing of a cheque is delayed because of inaccurate information contained in the application form. The perfect situation would be if we could have all the application forms in and they were all accurate. If that were the case, I suspect that cheques could be issued within a four week period. I am suggesting here that that would be the perfect situation, but not likely to occur.
The Hon. Member or Algoma (Mr. Foster) asked about the special entry in respect of administration, public information, and so on. He was correct; it would represent the total amount required to deliver the $ 1 billion package.
His other question was also raised by one of his colleagues. It concerned the questions raised and the information supplied to us within the last few days from soybean producers. It should be noted that those producers were part of the farm delegation which drafted and designed the formula. They have no criticism to make of the formula. However, we must bear in mind that the formula was a compromise of East and West

They certainly came together with more accuracy, understanding, and compassion than perhaps could politicians and bureaucrats. We should recognize it and compliment them on it. In any event, they came together, and the formula included seeded acreage, productivity, value of the grain, and regional yields. When we talk about regional yields, we cannot go beyond the accurate information in our possession in respect of crop insurance. We cannot go to the individual farmer because we do not have that information. In any event, they knew it and agreed with it.
Another component was the hurt factor. We must bear in mind that the criteria must be very clear. Farmers were very strong on the point that to qualify a commodity had to be directly and detrimentally affected by the U.S. Farm Bill and the trade war between the U.S. and the EEC. If one can meet that criterion, then one is in; if not, one is out. Whatever one does, one should not try to bootleg in any other commodity which does not meet the criterion.
Another overriding fact was that it was a massive program. We were breaking new ground, and we had nothing upon which to rely. However, we will work together with a fair and equitable formula of distribution. As far as I was concerned and as far as they were concerned, we would see no particular commodity group so that we could make calculations based upon returning the greatest benefit to it. Also we would see no provincial or regional boundary so that we could make the calculation based upon, for example, an extra $1 million being received by a province or region. However, we would work together to develop a formula which included these various components. We would build them in and factor them in, not to reflect the exact bushel or exact dollar, but to reflect regional yields, prices of commodities, and so on.
They wanted us to pick the base period. In picking the base period, we picked the best yield, the best three years out of five years. I thought that was fair; they thought that was fair.
As far as price is concerned and getting back to the hurt factor, we did not have the latitude to use a five-year average because it had to be directly tied to the U.S. Farm Bill. With all the highs and lows in commodities over the last five years, four years were prior to the introduction of the U.S. Farm Bill. The ups and downs were a result of everything else other than the U.S. Farm Bill. We were pretty well restricted, not so much by choice but by necessity, in picking the price decline in the 1986 crop. We could not use a five-year average at all.
While dealing with the five year average, let me talk about the position of the soybean people in their briefing material supplied to us. Incidentally, I met with them for an hour. I would have spent a little more time with them, but the bell was ringing and I had to leave. I think they were satisfied. However, when we announced the program we said that no agricultural program would be cut and that no agricultural funding would be reduced. There was some scepticism across the country that we would take into account the $800 and
Supply
some odd million paid under western grain stabilization, and that we would take into account the $50 million to $55 million-and I stand to be corrected on that amount-paid under agricultural stabilization to corn and soybean producers in the East. It was very clear from the beginning that we had to exclude those. They have nothing to do with the formula.
We must take into account the difficulty in dealing with a formula and throwing in different grains. Let us look for a moment at the Agricultural Stabilization Act, which all rural Members will know is 90 per cent of a five-year average adjusted for the cost of production. That is the ASA formula. If we take that formula and throw in corn, it triggers out at an ASA payment of $8.92 per tonne. If we take the same formula and throw in soybeans, it triggers out almost twice as high- $15.53 per tonne. Indeed that is the way it should work. Although feed grains are tied together in some respects, if we use the same formula and throw in two different grains, it will trigger two different amounts. Western grain stabilization had nothing to do with the formula whatsoever, and producers accepted that.
There are two ways in which to deal with the hurt factor. First, we could take the exact decline in the U.S. loan rate, which is known. It impacts in a certain way, with a certain pattern, on various grains under the program. We must also consider the drop in Canadian commodity prices. If we look at that line, it moves differently in certain commodities. We thought we should take a lesson from farmers. When they were faced with bigger challenges to try to incorporate, offset, balance, and equalize, they built in these factors along the way. We thought we should take a lesson from them, and we simply averaged the U.S. loan rate and the decline in Canadian commodity prices; that is what we did. In doing that, like the ASA formula, it triggered almost double. For example, we can take the Special Canadian Grains Program and throw in all these commodities. If we throw in corn, it triggers out at 34 cents per bushel. If we throw in soybeans, they trigger out at 19 cents.
I undertook to recalculate for purposes of, shall I say, reverifying that the factors used to determine the accuracy of the drop in Canadian commodity prices-not the loan rate because that is, shall I say, carved in stone although I hope it is ice and melts rapidly-or the hurt factor in other grains was the same as that applied to soybeans. You will have noticed that when we announced this program we set out final calculations. If we can utilize the time from now until the deadline of March 31 to improve the accuracy of the hurt factor, then we will attempt to do that. It may or may not change things but I think we have to satisfy ourselves on it because the farmers themselves are very strong on urgency and very high on accuracy as it relates to actual hurt. We will utilize the time we have to ensure that greater equity and fairness are built into the formula.

It is important that we maintain our expenditures within the fiscal framework. If we do not, we will send bad signals to the financial community throughout the world. A rise in interest rates of 1 per cent imposes an added cost of $140 million on the farm community.

These things are not carved in stone, but we must have something upon which to calculate. The best information is sought to do the calculations, the averages and so on, and these are estimates.
Furthermore, it is rather irrelevant because the important consideration will be after the deadline when we get the applications and the figures. Only then will we know exactly how many applied and how much grain was marketed. Then we will be in a position to issue the final financial assistance.

Mr. Chairman, I recognize the difficulty but I was just questioning the accuracy of the $5,000 figure because I suspect that it is not what it will be.
Will the Minister try to do something about the image that is being presented in some of the information presently being given?

Mr. Chairman, the average is just about as irrelevant. How does one determine who is an average farmer? That can only be done with a calculator which gives figures
but does not describe an average farmer. That is why we are saying that the typical farmer is the Rosetown, Saskatchewan example of a farmer receiving slightly over $9,000 and a Kent County typical farmer who, including his cropping pattern, receives almost the same as his counterpart in Rosetown, Saskatchewan.
I do not believe there is anything misleading about the chart. It shows revenue and income. People will know that cash receipts and gross income provide certain figures but that the bottom line is the net income. There is no reference to the net on the chart, as I recall it. I do not believe there is any confusion.

Mr. Chairman, perhaps in order to accommodate a faster schedule the Minister could respond to a number of my questions together. He stated earlier that he would distribute the application forms and other material but he will recognize that particularly for some farmers in eastern Canada, it will not be as easily accomplished as elsewhere. That I believe to be quite true. In the spirit of trying to make this plan work for as many people as possible, and given the time the Minister himself has indicated for a deadline for applications, I wonder if it would be possible for the Minister to identify those Hon. Members who would be interested in receiving the applications at their offices so we could take them to our constituency offices. And would the Minister consider drafting or having prepared a camera-ready sheet for our constituency mail-outs? I realize that not many Hon. Members will be interested in a camera-ready sheet, but it will be used by those Members of Parliament who represent the agriculture areas. In my view, given the importance of this issue and given the fact of what could happen if a farmer missed the deadline, and given the general willingness on the part of everyone to make this work, I think the Minister should consider having his staff prepare such a camera-ready sheet, as some Ministers do on occasion, provided it is not too partisan and something which everyone could use.
I know the Minister will give that suggestion the appropriate consideration. I would not ask to draft it for him because he may consider that partisan in another way. I hope the Minister would consider as well the circulation of the application forms to constituency offices or parliamentary offices so Members of Parliament can take them back to their ridings. These are cooperative things we can do together which will go a long way to assisting our farmers. Could the Minister respond to that suggestion and then I will raise the other issues about which I am concerned?

Mr. Chairman, that very matter was brought to my attention just a few moments ago by my colleagues, the Hon. Member for Bruce-Grey and the Hon. Member for Lambton-Middlesex. I appreciate the request made by my colleague and I see no reason why that cannot be done.
December 18, 1986

I am happy to hear that, Mr. Chairman. I only hope we can get that organized very shortly. The difficulty we have sometimes with camera-ready kits is that we receive them much too late and by then we have already sent out the constituency mail-out. As the Minister knows, there are only four mail-outs per year so the sooner we could get the camera-ready sheet, the better. We could time the next constituency mail-out around the end of January, which is what I am looking forward to right now, and if I could include that sheet in bilingual format, I would be grateful.
I have a few other questions for the Minister and I wonder if I could have his undivided attention for a few moments, if he does not mind so I could get some response to my questions. I wonder if the Minister could tell us how the program is going to work for the corn producers. I would like to know specifically which groups will be included and which will be excluded. The Minister and 1 have had some private conversations about that subject earlier and I understand his officials have looked into the matter.
Will the high moisture corn producers be included and, if so, how is it going to work? It is a kind of difficult area, or at least it is perceived that way. There are a number of cob corn producers in my constituency and practically everywhere throughout Ontario. I am sure there are some in the Minister's own riding. I would like to know whether they are included. Could he give us more detail as to who is included and who is excluded and how we are going to run the program for high moisture corn producers? Are the cob corn producers going to be covered? Would the Minister respond to those questions, please?

Yes, Mr. Chairman, all corn producers will be eligible. High moisture corn will be eligible because high moisture corn is harvested as a grain. The only thing which will be excluded is, in farmers' terms, "ensilage". To upgrade that term, perhaps we could call it silage. Using a more modern term, I suppose we could say all plant silage would be excluded. However, high moisture corn and high moisture barley are harvested as a grain and would be included.

I did not hear specifically about cob corn, but I gather that when the Minister said "all corn producers", that would automatically be included. I see a nod which tells me that that would be the case.
I wonder if I could turn to one more issue? Since this is an appropriation Bill, I suppose we can deviate somewhat from the central issue. With respect to the corn producers, the Minister will know that a number of corn producers in Ontario are worried about the countervail on U.S. corn. There are two aspects they feel are potentially deficient. First, the Minister will know that the countervail was placed rather late. I thought it was interesting when the Minister said he was far more interested in cropping years than calendar years or any other kinds of years. I could not help but ask myself why his colleague, the Minister of National Revenue (Mr. MacKay), could not have that same concern when we in fact had that
Supply
delay in putting in place the countervail on U.S. corn. While I appreciate the fact that the Minister himself is well aware that agriculture is seasonal and that he has to bear that in mind when he makes any decision, it seems to me that some of his colleagues, particularly the Minister of National Revenue, forgot abut that part of the equation not all that long ago.
The delay in placing the countervail on U.S. corn was from September 30 to, I believe, November 14. One of the difficulties we had at that time was that during the last 10 days prior to the countervail, as much corn came into the country as the previous year. I wonder if the Minister could tell us, first, if he has asked his colleague to consider the possibility, recognizing it would be difficult, of retroactively imposing a tariff on that corn. I know it is sometimes hard to trace and it would not be possible in all cases. Nevertheless, was that considered and, if so, what was the result? Second, the tariff on corn, I understand, initially only applied to grain corn but did not apply to ground products. Has there been a modification since to ensure that ground corn and other forms of corn products are also covered by the countervail so that in fact we are not giving the opportunity to an American exporter to use some other method to send it in and bypass the tariff altogether? Perhaps the Minister could respond to those questions?

Mr. Chairman, I think the Hon. Member is unduly critical and considerably unfair to my colleague, the Minister of National Revenue (Mr. MacKay), in his comments. As he knows, the Import Tribunal is a quasi-judicial body and quite properly separate and apart from any political interference or intervention. It was a very complicated study and there was a positive determination rendered by the Import Tribunal as a preliminary determination. We will not know the final determination until February.
The Hon. Member mentioned the fact that imports rolled across the border in a very short period of time. I have had that question raised before and have inquired about it. To this point in time the information I have is that it is difficult to substantiate that claim. If the Hon. Member has some additional information which would be helpful, I would appreciate if he would supply it to me. There are observations and sometimes the observations are accurate, sometimes they are not. I would not say that it is not true. The information I have is that it cannot be substantiated, and therein lies our problem.

The question which the Hon. Member raises about the corn countervail is a matter which has been dealt with. It was dealt with retroactively to November 7, 1986, in terms of the kernel as a whole, cracked corn, crushed corn, ground corn, rolled corn, sliced corn and corn screenings. It appears that the concern in the mind of the Hon. Member has been dealt with, as usual, with great completeness and satisfaction by the Government.

Mr. Chairman, I have but one last question. The Minister answered every question except the one I asked him just a moment ago which is the following one. Why was the countervail tariff not imposed retroactively until September 30 which was the date when the original decision was supposed to have been made? As far as I am concerned that is the date of the original decision. It was considered fair game for anyone who had shipped up until that time. However, there were those who shipped in the interval between September 30 and November 14. I ask the Minister why the tariff was not imposed retroactively to September 30. That seems like the proper thing to do. It would have assisted a great many farmers since it is at a time of year when the product is sold.

Mr. Chairman, I want to be brief because I think we have only a few moments at our disposal. The Hon. Member knows that the Import Tribunal does not report to the Minister of Agriculture but to my colleague the Minister of National Revenue. I ask the Hon. Member to make representations to him. I am sure he will receive an answer.

Mr. Chairman, I believe we can allow the other clauses to pass if we can obtain an answer from the Minister to the question I put previously. The cost of professional and special services for getting this payment out is stated in the Blue Book which we do not have before us at this time. The Minister did not tell us what particular professional and special services there are which will cost $1.54 million, which figure is almost one-half of the total administration costs. There is an administration in place which should be able to handle a great deal of the informational process which goes on. In the West there are two separate administrations, the western grain stabilization administration and the Canadian Wheat Board. We want to know why farmers will not be receiving this $1.5 million. We want to know why so much money is required for professional and special services. The Minister did not really outline what it was for in his previous attempt at an answer.

Mr. Chairman, it is true that we have a communications branch in place, which has obviously done a good job. The message I have received from our communications people is that because of the size of this program they will need additional help and it may be of a professional nature. That is the only way I can answer the Hon. Member's question.

Mr. Chairman, will the Minister assure us that this money will not be some type of political grant to groups which do public relations for the Conservative Party? Will the Minister assure us that this money will not be used to print a bunch of slick brochures extolling the Conservative Party but that it will be for the dissemination of straight information? Why does it cost so much to put out straight
information when there are these various administrations in place in both the East and the West which are designed to carry out this function and which can do it at no extra cost?

Mr. Chairman, I made an inquiry with respect to this matter some three or four days ago. I was told that the biggest information program which is put out other than with respect to the cranking out of press releases is worth about $15,000 and more money is needed. I am sure that anything that goes out will be stamped "Government of Canada" or "Agriculture Canada". speechtext:
that the Bill be read the third time and passed.
She said: Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to be able to conclude our deliberations on Bill C-25. I wish to thank Hon. Members opposite for their co-operation in this respect. By passing this legislation, the sale of Canadair to Bombardier can now be concluded, which brings to eight the number of divestitures carried out by our Government.
There are a number of key elements in the sale of Canadair which I would like to re-emphasize. First, the Government believes it is sound public policy to manage Crown corporations efficiently. In the case of Canadair, state ownership had seriously handicapped the firm from keeping up with a fast-moving and technologically changing competitive aerospace industry. Therefore, the purpose of this privatization was not to solve the many problems of the past but rather to create for the company and its employees the best possible future. This legislation provides the authority to carry out the final step in returning Canadair to the private sector where it has the potential to grow as a dynamic and competitive business operation.

Second, when it negotiated this sale, the Government was not interested in the selling price alone. Our vision of a more brilliant future for Canadair had to consider other factors that would create maximum social and economic benefits. The sale of Canadair to Bombardier will be instrumental in doing so, in a number of ways. Certain aspects of the transaction, such as Bombardier's commitment to maintain Canadair's manufacturing facilities and its headquarters in Quebec will ensure that Canadair plays a major role in the aerospace sector in Quebec and across the country.
Furthermore, a special share issue will help increase research and development activity at Canadair, thus encouraging expansion of export markets and increasing the use of Canadian products.
Finally, the Government was impressed by Bombardier's financial discipline, management and competence on the international market, all of which have made Bombardier a leader in transportation technology, both in Canada and
Canadair Limited Divestiture Act
abroad. This alliance between Bombardier and Canadair guarantees a far better future for Canadair and its employees.
If there are any doubts about employment potential with Bombardier, let me remind Hon. Members that The Financial Post has ranked Bombardier as one of Canada's best employers in terms of productivity and job satisfaction. In sum, the purchase of Canadair by Bombardier creates a fertile environment for growth through the merging of Canadair's technology and skilled workforce with Bombardier's management expertise and international marketing experience.
We firmly believe that it is private enterprise that should be engaged in the business of designing, producing and marketing aircraft. That is why we decided to privatize Canadair. The sale of Canadair is just one example of the action the Government has taken to better manage our public assets and fully realize their economic potential.
The international market-place is becoming increasingly competitive and fast moving. This is particularly true in the aerospace sector. Canadair, in concert with Bombardier, will now be in a position to make the most of those new challenges and opportunities that are natural to an industry which thrives on change.
The sale of de Havilland to Boeing is an example of another successful privatization. De Havilland has just landed its biggest order of Dash 8 aircraft yet. In June, orders were placed by a group of Canadian carriers for 42 Dash 8 aircraft. Since then, de Havilland obtained orders and options for another 132.

Mr. Speaker, we believe that Bombardier will bring to Canadair the kind of creative management that has made it a leader in transportation development, both in this country and abroad. This should give Canadair the new direction it needs to compete effectively.
Bombardier has the necessary financial resources and experience to meet the challenge of selling a complex product on foreign markets. The merger of Canadair with Bombardier will give the Canadian aerospace industry a unique opportunity to increase research and development in this sector, to increase Canadian content and supplier competence, to increase Canadian exports and to assist Canadair's customers on all markets related to the aerospace industry.
We firmly believe that returning Canadair to the private sector is in the best interests of the Company and this country.

It has been a pleasure for me to work on this Bill, to present it, to debate it and to conclude deliberations which will ensure speedy passage of the Canadair Limited Divestiture Authorization Act. On behalf of the Government and the employees of Canadair, I thank Hon. Members for recognizing the urgency

December 18, 1986
Canadair Limited Divestiture Act
and importance of this legislation and for assisting the Government in giving Canadair the opportunity to achieve the excellence that will build its future.
[ Translation]

Mr. Speaker, I do not intend to take much of the time of the House this afternoon because we all want the debate on this Bill to end very quickly.
First of all, Mr. Speaker, as you know we are not necessarily against the sale of Canadair to Bombardier. We are pleased to note that the Government did not repeat the same mistakes it made in the past, particularly with respect to the sale of de Havilland and the divestiture of Canadian Arsenals. We are aware of the mistakes made in the case of de Havilland.
As to Canadian Arsenals, a number of mistakes had been made when tenders were first called, so they had to start all over again a few times. And then the other major mistake, in my opinion, is that the employees of Canadian Arsenals had practically been forgotten.
Indeed, after lengthy negotiations which led to a rather acrimonious debate in the House of Commons, the unions, the new employer and the Government finally reached an agreement at the last minute.
I do hope there will be no such problems in this case.
It seems that Canadair employees are definitely more satisfied than was the case in the sale of the other two Crown corporations-where I was involved to a certain extent- certainly more so than the employees of Canadian Arsenals who showed their discontent.
Mr. Speaker, one interesting fact should be noted.

It is nice to remember Conservative Party promises on many occasions. Perhaps I could take a moment to reflect upon a promise that was made on August 15, 1984, by the present Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson). During the election campaign, while he was a member of the Opposition, he said that a Conservative Government would turn Canadair Limited and de Havilland Aircraft of Canada Limited into a separate Crown corporation. I am sure it would surprise you a great deal, Mr. Speaker, if I said that the Government has broken another promise. However, that is something for which Conservatives have been rather well known.
In the case of this promise, perhaps the moral is that it should not have been made to begin with. However, it is for the Tories to think about those kinds of things in the future and to stop promising things that they either do not intend to deliver, should not be delivering, or have no intention of delivering.

speakerposition: Minister of State (Fitness and Amateur Sport)
speechtext: What hogwash.
The amateur Minister of fitness and sport is saying hogwash, or is it the Minister of Fitness and Amateur Sport?

speakerposition: Minister of State (Fitness and Amateur Sport)
speechtext: You don't know what you're talking about at any time.

Whichever. I will not debate extensively with the amateur Minister across the way because he knows as well what promises were made.

Mr. Speaker, I end my remarks by saying that, unlike other Crown corporations, Canadair is definitely not a deficit-ridden concern. Indeed I think it has been operating on a fairly sound financial basis, and we know that its projected net profits for this year are about $23.8 million, so it has to be in good financial shape.
I certainly hope that Bombardier officials-well known for their sound management, as the Minister pointed out earlier- will be able to keep Canadair operating in the black, in their own interest and in the interest of the employees who should not be forgotten in all these dealings. Too often in such cases- I gave examples a few minutes ago-Canadians who have been working for these Crown corporations for many years have been left in the dark. They were not even involved in negotiations in the past and I hope... I am told that the employees are much more satisfied in this case. Perhaps they are not fully satisfied, but still I hope everything will turn out all right for them, that their pension fund and working conditions will be adequately protected. There is one thing about which I am still not convinced, and I would like to know whether Bombardier company officials intend to relocate their facilities elsewhere in Quebec. We know the Minister said earlier that the Corporation was going to keep its facilities in Quebec. But even with that, there could still be some disadvantages for employees if there were to be any moves to other parts of the province.
Mr. Speaker, I would like to take just a few moments, but not any longer than necessary, to talk about this issue and some of our concerns. Some of my colleagues have other concerns and they would like to express them, but they are not in a position to do so right now, since we have agreed to adopt this Bill fairly quickly. Nevertheless, I would like to take a few moments to bring these concerns to the attention of the House.

Mr. Speaker, I rise to say a few words as the debate on privatization of Canadair is wound down. I regret the haste with which we have been required to move on this Bill for obvious reasons in terms of legalities to facilitate the transfer. But there is a much greater dicussion that ought to take place, and perhaps with the Minister of State for Privatization (Mrs. McDougall) here, I would urge that she consider that, if we do move again in this direction at the eleventh hour, we do not rush debate and rush things through committee.
We are dealing with the profoundly important matter of privatization, which in my mind stems from an ideological commitment by members of the government Party to have to
December 18, 1986

privatize something because it makes them feel good to privatize. There may be good reasons why certain Crown corporations should be privatized. I do not speak against the principle. But I must remind the Minister that, in spite of her best efforts, while I might not agree with what she is doing she is soldiering on with privatization.
It is interesting to note, on looking at the amount of private and public ownership in Canada today, and comparing with the situation on September 4, 1984, that there is more public ownership today than ever before. Federal public ownership is greater today than when the Conservatives took office. This is interesting in itself because of the myth which you, Mr. Speaker, know as well as I do that we are privatizing the various Crown corporations and that we are moving to less and less public ownership. In fact, by the Government's own action in taking over Petro-Canada's Gulf stations we have expanded public ownership. So that we are all perfectly clear as to exactly what has happened, as opposed to the mythology of what is happening, public ownership is actually on the increase thanks to the actions of this Government.
In a country as vast as ours with a small population we have always appreciated that there is a role for the public sector to play, whether it is in a national airline, railroad, or going back to 1821 with the construction of the Lachine Canal.
As a student of history yourself, Mr. Speaker, you will know that the Lachine Canal being built by the private sector could not be completed. The company went bankrupt and did not succeed in this venture. As it was defined at that time, for the best interests of Canada, the Government of the day stepped in and said that the canal had to be built because it is important to the country. If the private sector cannot or will not do it, the Government must. So it stepped into one of the first public enterprises in Canada, which was the completion of the Lachine Canal after the failure of the private sector.
I use that historic example as one that shows that there is indeed a role. In looking at the action of Conservative Governments over the years, both federally and provincially, public ownership has become a natural tool to develop certain utilities for the public good, whether it is Alberta Telephone, B.C. Hydro, Ontario Hydro, or whether it is to launch an airline like Pacific Western Airlines which has now taken over Canadian Pacific Airlines. People in the Government perceive that these are good steps and that they are in the interest of western Canada.
The other example is a better one, that of Air Canada.
Get is straight among yourselves.

Pacific Western is a public airline primarily owned by the people of western Canada. It has now taken over CP Air which was a privately owned airline. In Canada there are two publicly owned airlines, one is Pacific Western and the other one is called Air Canada. Wardair is out there soldiering on.

speechtext: I did the financing for that-in the private sector.

I will close off this discussion of the privatization of Canadair by saying-and I guess it is serving notice-that we are going against what every other country in the aerospace industry has done. Public participation in the aerospace industries of France, West Germany, United Kingdom, and all countries involved in an aerospace business perceive government participation in one way or another as being absolutely natural and essential.
The one exception to the rule is the United States. But that country's vast involvement in the armed forces must be considered. After all, the development of its aerospace industry is done through its military budgets, which is another way of saying that the Government of the United States is obviously a critical key and major player in the development of its aerospace industry.
The Minister of State for Privatization states that this is something that must be done. Every other country in the world that is involved in the aerospace business does not particularly have that view. They do not have this ideological need to privatize something, which in this case is Canadair. However, the deed is done. The majority Government has decided that this is one thing that it must do before it leaves office in two years. So be it.
I wish to complete my comments by saying that by the Government's own figures we are only guaranteed to receive payments totalling $149 million for Canadair with a further $8 million to $12 million in contingency payments, compared to the book value of Canadair which is pegged at $224 million for 1985. This figure was provided by CDIC itself. As taxpayers of the country, we are not really getting a very good deal. In fact, this is a nice Christmas present to be passed along to the private sector.
The sale at this price also comes at a time of increasing profitability forecast for the company. Profits for 1983 were $6 million. That was a very difficult year. In 1985, the profits were $27.5 million and the 1986 forecast is for $23.8 million. After much investment, time, technology, energy and talent, we see the fruits of those investments; and just when things are turning around and looking good for Canadair it is being sold off to Bombardier. It is getting a real bargain in this deal.
Prior to the sale, Canadair had been promised major federal government support totalling $50 million, $30.9 million in defence industry production program assistance for the production of the CL-227 systems, and another $20 million for a joint venture with West Germany on the CL-289. It was virtually promised another $30 million in DIPP money by the letter of intent in the sale of the company, and $14 million for the CL-215 water bomber, $10 million in modifications to the Challenger, and $5 million for new equipment.
Time does not permit me to go on describing this unbelievably good deal. The Government is sugar-coating this whole

December 18, 1986
Canadair Limited Divestiture Act
deal to facilitate the transfer to Bombardier. A lot of champagne will be drunk in the boardrooms of Bombardier tonight. A good company is getting a fantastic deal from the Government. Of course, the people who will not be celebrating will be Canadian taxpayers. Once again tonight they will remember the Avro Arrow. Tonight people will be sitting in their livingrooms, kitchens, and dens; they will be thinking about the Avro Arrow. They will remember that just as Canada was beginning to make a breakthrough in the aerospace industry, the Government pulled the rug out from under that industry. Was it a Conservative or a Liberal Government at that time?
It was a Conservative Government.

It was a Conservative Government at that time, and a Conservative Government is doing it again. The Avro Arrow will be haunting Canadians again tonight, as there are celebrations in the boardrooms of Bombardier because of this incredible Christmas present. I have no further comments to make.
