speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Employment and Immigration
maintopic: UNEMPLOYMENT INSURANCE ACT, 1971 MEASURE TO AMEND
speechtext:
That is another great relief.

Mr. Speaker, Hon. Members of this House, I would like to submit for your consideration today a Bill that contains two important amendments to the Unemployment Insurance Act.

These amendments, if passed into law, will freeze the UI premium rate for 1987 and will extend the variable entrance rate for another year.
The Bill recognizes the sensitivity of the Government to regional differences in Canada, to the financial pressures on Canadians workers across the country, and to the consequences of increased costs to small business, recognizing that small business is responsible for maintaining and creating economic recovery in Canada.
The UI program plays a vital role in our society. Its benefits replace lost income. They help maintain the stability of local economies, and they also help protect the jobs of people employed in those communities. The ability of individuals to meet the basic expenses of food and shelter while they look for another job is maintained by UI benefits.
For some time, especially over the last several months, there has been much discussion about UI. Many different aspects of the program have been both criticized and praised. Business, labour, women's organizations, and many other groups are asking whether the program is fair and efficient. Is it impeding
December 18, 1986

the development of new jobs? Is it doing enough to provide unemployed Canadians with new opportunities?
As a Government, we clearly recognize that unemployment insurance is a critical element in the Canadian employment system. Supported primarily by the premiums of individual businesses and their employees, the program belongs to Canadians in a more direct sense than any other government program. The Government is simply a trustee whose role is to manage public funds on behalf of Canadians.
Recently the Minister of Employment and Immigration (Mr. Bouchard) received the Forget Commission Report of inquiry into the Unemployment Insurance Commission and its workings. It will be the Government's job to take a look at the report and to consider other reports such as the Macdonald Commission Report and the House report from Newfoundland. It is also its job to strike an equitable balance between the recommendations of various groups and interests across Canada.
Returning to the Bill itself, Bill C-16 proposes to amend the Act to freeze the premium rate at its present level until December 31, 1987, that is, S2.35 for workers and $3.29 for employers for each $100 of insurable benefits. The formula now in place, if left unchanged, would require the Government to raise the premium rate again for next year. Employees would have to pay as much as $2.50 for every $100 of insurable earnings. Employers would have to pay more, approximately 1.4 per cent more for each employee. For the coming year alone, these equate to approximately $625 million worth of contributions which will not be taken away from employees and employers. It is an important factor which should not be taken lightly.
The Government believes that if it had allowed the premium to jump, as the formula required, it would throw a monkey-wrench into the economic recovery we in Canada are now enjoying. In addition, our calculations indicate that the decision to maintain premiums at the present level will not unduly impede the longer term reduction in the cumulative unemployment insurance account deficit. The decision to hold the line on UI premiums shows how we are willing to listen to and respond to the concerns of the business community, and at the same time respect financial pressures on individual Canadian workers through reduced premiums and increased benefits.
The Government cares about Canadians who are disadvantaged, discriminated against, and caught in the web of economic misery. We have a social conscience.
The freezing of the UI premium rate helps to give stability to employer-employee costs. It will also remove the financial burden on both employers and workers, the major shareholders of the UI account.
In addition to the question of premium rates, there is a more urgent need to extend the variable entrance requirements, or the VER, until January 4, 1988. On January 4, 1987 the VER is due to expire. The VER first came into effect in December,
Canadair Limited Divestiture Act
1977. It allows UI claimants to qualify for benefits based upon the difficulty of finding and keeping work. It is based upon the unemployment rate in each of the 48 economic regions of Canada.
The VER recognizes that it is more difficult to find and to keep a job in areas suffering from high unemployment. Hon. Members from British Columbia, Newfoundland, and even Alberta know how important this will be to their constituents and other Canadian workers. In an economic region with a high level of unemployment, a claimant needs as few as 10 weeks of insurable work to qualify for UI benefits, as long as the VER is in place. If the VER is allowed to expire, all claimants will need a minimum of 14 weeks to qualify for UI benefits. That would create a hardship for as many as 208,000 Canadians. In areas of high unemployment they would find themselves without work, pay or UI. Bill C-16 contains an extension to the VER to allow the UI program to continue to respond to regional differences for the next 12 months, from January 4, 1987, until January 4, 1988. The extension will symbolize the Prime Minister's, the Government's, and ultimately Parliament's recognition of the difficulties many Canadians face in finding work.
Our decision to freeze the premium rate will help Canadians find new jobs by removing a potential barrier to growth. We do not want to create hardship so we are asking this House to approve these amendments quickly. For 1987 employers and workers will know what the UI program will cost them. And they will be able to plan accordingly. UI claimants will know if they qualify.

Those are the amendments that I am tabling before the House, Mr. Speaker. I ask Hon. Members to approve an extension of the variable entrance rate and a freeze on the premium rate for 1987. I would appreciate the co-operation of all Hon. Members in adopting these amendments without delay. Thank you very much.

Hon. Warren Allmand (Notre-Dame-de-Grace-Lachine
East): Mr. Speaker, as the Parliamentary Secretary said, C-16 is a simple Bill to extend the variable entrance requirements of the Unemployment Insurance Act and freeze the level of contributions for one more year. As Hon. Members know, the VER provides that an employee can qualify for unemployment insurance if he or she works for 10 to 14 weeks and makes contributions. They can qualify with 10 weeks of work if they live in a region where unemployment is over 9 per cent. The requirement increases from 10 to 14 weeks as the rate of unemployment declines below 9 per cent. This provision is in recognition of the fact that in some parts of Canada it is very difficult to find work and that is why we provide more unemployment insurance benefits in those regions.

December 18, 1986
While we support the Bill, I regret that the Government waited until the second to the last day before the Christmas recess to put it before us for debate. It raises many important issues with respect to unemployment insurance which members of my caucus wanted to discuss. If it is as important as the Parliamentary Secretary says it is, we should have had it before us for debate at least a week or so ago. That is particularly true since we have had the Forget Commission Report tabled.
In debating this Bill I must point out the confusion that reigns with respect to the Government's policy on unemployment insurance. After the election, the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) and the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) said that changes in the unemployment insurance program are necessary and there must be a review. They set up the Forget Commission on Unemployment Insurance. However, while that commission was sitting the Government brought in very serious changes to the program. It cut unemployment insurance for workers who took a pre-retirement pension. That affected almost 76,000 Canadians who paid into the program for years and years but then could not collect the amounts owing to them.
Finally we got the commission report on December 3.1 must say that it was a very confusing report because there were six members of the commission and a minority report was produced. What does the Government do? After a year and a half of study by the commission it will not have a response to the report until May 15, five months later. However, it did respond to one of the recommendations, number 26, which we support, that the Government should rescind the cuts relating to pre-retirement pensions as of January 5 of this year and reimburse those workers who should have received full unemployment insurance. So the one recommendation the Government responded to was rejected. Yet the Government had been telling this House for months on end that it would deal with that issue when the commission reported. The Prime Minister said that. The Minister of Employment and Immigration (Mr. Bouchard) said that. The Minister of Finance said that, and so did the Associate Minister of National Defence (Mr. Dick). Over and over again we were told to wait for the Forget Commission Report and then the Government would deal with those cuts. No wonder there is confusion with respect to the Government's unemployment insurance policy.
As to the VER which this Bill deals with, recommendation number 23 of the Forget Commission Report rejected it. I was pleased today to hear the Parliamentary Secretary give very good reasons for maintaining the VER. How the Government will respond to that recommendation I do not know.
In the last two weeks a certain consensus has been developing with respect to unemployment insurance and the Forget Commission Report. The direction seems to be that we should postpone for a considerable period of time the recommendation for annualization and cutting of the regional extended benefits.
Even the commissioners themselves, when they appeared before the Standing Committee on Labour, Employment and Immigration, agreed we should not go ahead with those until we have in place a very specific plan for income support and regional development. There is in fact consensus on a lot of the recommendations in the report.
In conclusion I would like to repeat that we support this Bill but strongly suggest that the Government clean up its act on unemployment insurance and rescind the cuts for preretirement pensioners. It should put off consideration of the recommendation relating to annualization and regional extended benefits until a very specific alternative plan for income support and regional development is put in place. The Government should bring in a Bill on those areas where there is consensus. We do not need five more months to do that.

Mr. Speaker, as Chairman of the Liberal Party task force on postsecondary education, I have heard from educators across Canada that our universities are in danger of becoming second class. Those words are ringing through today. McMaster University has announced that it is being forced to cancel its Canadian studies program because of the lack of government funding. The real irony of this situation is that the cancellation will be effective Canada Day, 1987. Does the Government wish to celebrate Canada Day by cancelling Canadian studies programs throughout the land?
Situations such as what is happening at McMaster University are eroding the quality of education in Canada. If this is allowed to continue, knowledge of our country will be further eroded, and Canadians will be handicapped in competing internationally. The Government should and must take affirmative action now to eliminate the erosion of our educational system. Otherwise, the Government will be single-handedly responsible for making Canada a second class nation. Is this the type of legacy the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) wants to leave the Canadian people?
December 18, 1986

subtopic: FEDERAL-PROVINCIAL AGREEMENT DESIGNATING BRITISH COLUMBIA PACIFIC CENTRE FOR TRADE, COMMERCE AND TRAVEL
FEDERAL-PROVINCIAL AGREEMENT DESIGNATING BRITISH COLUMBIA PACIFIC CENTRE FOR TRADE, COMMERCE AND TRAVEL
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would like to draw to the attention of the House an agreement signed on Tuesday between the federal Government and the Government of the Province of British Columbia promoting the development of British Columbia as Canada's Pacific centre for trade, commerce, and travel. The agreement will allow the two Governments to co-ordinate initiatives to enhance British Columbia's future economic development.
These include encouraging the growth of international banking and other financial services in Vancouver, coordinating transportation improvements, enhancing trade-related services and greater trade opportunities in those professional and technical services where British Columbians have developed significant expertise, and improving coordination of marketing and promotion of British Columbia as a tourist destination.
A joint management committee will advise the two Governments on these and other initiatives compatible with British Columbia's special designation as Canada's Pacific gateway. This agreement reaffirms the Government's commitment, as outlined in the Throne Speech, to assist in the renewal and diversification of the economy of British Columbia.

subtopic: FUTURE OF CENTRAL POST OFFICE IN PRINCE ALBERT
FUTURE OF CENTRAL POST OFFICE IN PRINCE ALBERT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, less than two months ago Canada Post Corporation brought down a business plan which recommends the closing of many rural post offices and the privatization of many postal services. Just last Thursday DPW informed the architects that Canada Post would no longer require space in the new federal building being planned for Prince Albert. There is no doubt that the two incidents are related, that Canada Post has decided that the downtown Prince Albert Post Office will either be privatized or will provide reduced service.
The people of Prince Albert and region require a central post office which can provide good service. That service is being threatened. What would my predecessor, the Right Hon. John Diefenbaker, say if he knew that the Government was tampering with Her Majesty's mail in the city of Prince Albert?

subtopic: PLIGHT OF IRANIAN STUDENT FACING DEPORTATION FROM UNITED STATES
PLIGHT OF IRANIAN STUDENT FACING DEPORTATION FROM UNITED STATES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as the House approaches the Christmas break it is most regrettable that the Minister of State (Immigration) (Mr. Weiner) has ignored the pleas of and for Akbar Moatamedi. The 25-year old Iranian student faces deportation from the United States on January 7. It is guaranteed to be a one-way journey to his persecution and probable death at the hands of Iranian authorities.
Such a frightening conclusion does not augur well for the spirit of the festive season. It does not augur well for the Government's self-proclaimed humanitarian immigration policy. It does not augur well for the Canadians in Yarmouth, Nova Scotia, who have desperately tried to sponsor this young man as a refugee. It certainly does not augur well for Akbar, who said in a telephone conversation from Washington: "I am living with a knife at my throat, waiting for someone to push it in".
Parliament and the Government can save this man from his sad and terrifying state. It is my hope that the Minister and the Government will be moved by the Christmas spirit which surrounds us all to extend a compassionate hand to an individual whose time is quickly and, regrettably, running out.

Mr. Speaker, the year 1986 which will wind up in a few days from now has been a banner year, both economically and socially in Temis-camingue's development and growth.
We had in 1986 a Social and Economic Summit in our area, the impressive celebrations of Ville-Marie's Centenary and the Fifth International Movie Festival. All of which points to our pride and commitment to realize and control our destinies.
Moreover, Mr. Speaker, let me take this opportunity to thank all the agencies and volunteers who continiously work for the promotion of Temiscamingue's development.
In conclusion, Mr. Speaker, may I wish all my fellow citizens, you and all Hon. Members a very merry Christmas season.
2254

December 18, 1986

subtopic: TREATMENT OF WORKERS FACING LAY-OFFS AT CANADA PACKERS PLANT IN WINNIPEG
TREATMENT OF WORKERS FACING LAY-OFFS AT CANADA PACKERS PLANT IN WINNIPEG
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as many Members will know, in the new year some 447 people at Canada Packers in Winnipeg will lose their jobs as a result of a decision taken by the Government to give $1 million to a competing plant in Neepawa.
I have two requests of the Government. First, will it consider making a special case of the lay-offs at Canada Packers and not count, for unemployment insurance purposes, the severance pay packages that workers will be receiving? It is a clear example of the injustices of that policy. The longer one works at a particular place and the more difficult it will be to make a transition, the less entitlement one has to unemployment insurance benefits.
Furthermore, using this as an example, will the Government reconsider its whole policy of counting severance pay packages for unemployment insurance benefits? It is very unfair, particularly to older workers who have worked at a particular place for a long time. They are the very people I and many others believe should be entitled to a greater cushion between the time they have lost their job and are able to find a new job.
I ask the Government to reconsider that policy. I know it has not, but it should.

maintopic: SUPPORT URGED FOR HEAVY OIL PROJECTS
SUPPORT URGED FOR HEAVY OIL PROJECTS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, Canada stands in danger of losing its lead in heavy oil technology if heavy oil projects and upgrader construction are postponed or cancelled.
One of the more serious issues is the loss to the energy industry of its talent to other businesses or countries. We may end up importing rather than exporting our technology. A recent Alberta Research Council study revealed that enhanced oil recovery and development of new in situ bitumen plants will be delayed, which brings about other important issues of energy self-sufficiency and security of supply. Oil imports could reach the dangerously high level of 1.45 million barrels a day within 15 years if new supplies are not found.
To quote a Calgary businessman: "Alberta runs on oil- when that stops, Alberta stops".

subtopic: REPORTED PLAN TO ABANDON MONTREAL-NORTH BAY MAIN LINE
REPORTED PLAN TO ABANDON MONTREAL-NORTH BAY MAIN LINE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, according to internal documents Canadian National Railways is planning to shut down many lines. An internal memo from R. P. Langlois, Regional Manager of Marketing in the St. Lawrence region, says in part:
In the context of the rationalization of our rail infrastructure, some lines have been identified as being potential candidates for abandonment in the coming years. A preliminary plan has been prepared and attached you will find the sections affected.
Any effort to attract new traffic on these sections is to be abandoned immediately.
One of the lines proposed to be abandoned is the main CN rail line between Montreal and North Bay. This would effectively eliminate VIA Rail between Ottawa and Montreal, plus any freight traffic. It would end many businesses in my riding.
Worst of all, CN proposes to do this in the year 1990. If that is not bad enough, the President of CN Rail wrote a letter to me in which he indicated that CN had no intention of shutting down the rail line. That is obviously contrary to the truth.

Mr. Speaker, some time ago the Toronto Star had an editorial entitled "Make Canada Post Visit Every Doorstep". More recently an Ottawa area municipality went to court to attempt to force Canada Post to deliver to every house.
What kind of a fool's world do these people live in? I can understand the Toronto Star, which rarely has a sensible stand on any issue, but I am disappointed by municipal politicians who would make such inane comments.
In my constituency of Prince Edward-Hastings there are 24 post offices. Only one community, Belleville, has door-to-door delivery. In every other instance citizens must walk to pick up their mail, and if they want to pick it up other than between nine and five they must pay extra for the privilege.
In the small village where I live, senior citizens must walk up to two kilometres winter and summer to pick up their mail. Other communities involve similar distances. I am no apologist for Canada Post. I have had as many delays and foul-ups reported to me as any Member and I am as frustrated as any with the services, but let us keep mail delivery in perspective.
December 18, 1986

subtopic: CALL FOR ESTABLISHMENT OF CHAIR IN SIKH STUDIES
CALL FOR ESTABLISHMENT OF CHAIR IN SIKH STUDIES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the establishment of chairs in ethnic studies at Canadian universities has been a far-sighted Canadian policy. Ethno-cultural communities have raised funds and the federal Government has matched the endowment for some 10 different chairs. Members of these communities take pride in one more contribution that they are able to make to Canadian life from their history and society.
Establishment of a chair in Sikh studies at the University of British Columbia would add to the cultural resources of that great university. It would also provide Sikhs in Canada generally, and particularly in British Columbia, with a Canadian focus for exploration of their religion and traditions. Such an establishment would, I am convinced, advance social harmony in Canada, which achievement should take precedence over external pressures. I call upon the Minister for Multiculturalism to authorize federal funding for a chair in Sikh studies.

subtopic: REPORT ON SUCCESS OF CANADIAN EFFORTS
REPORT ON SUCCESS OF CANADIAN EFFORTS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, recently I had the privilege to travel with the Standing Committee on External Affairs and International Trade to three developing countries as part of a review of Canada's foreign aid policy. It is the first major review in 15 years. I witnessed firsthand the goodwill generated by Canada's foreign aid and I am proud to know that our assistance has created a spirit of initiative and hope.
Canada is well recognized amongst industrialized nations for its official development assistance to less fortunate countries. The ODA Program has brought substantial economic returns to all regions of Canada. My province alone has helped to open new markets around the world in agriculture and potash.
We realize there are certain risks involved in development. However, with the guidance of NGO volunteers, these countries have a better opportunity to succeed in becoming self-sufficient and potential trading partners. I commend these individuals for their dedication in delivering aid to those who are critically in need. During this holiday season we should be proud to share our good fortune with those who are less fortunate.

subtopic: ONTARIO RESOLUTION RECOMMENDING INCLUSION OF PROPERTY RIGHTS
ONTARIO RESOLUTION RECOMMENDING INCLUSION OF PROPERTY RIGHTS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it was certainly good news yesterday when this House received from the Legislative Assembly of the Province of Ontario a copy of its resolution which would enshrine property rights in the Canadian Constitution. Until the Charter of Rights and Freedoms is amended to include the provision:
Everyone has the right to own and occupy property and the right not to be deprived thereof except in accordance with the principles of fundamental justice",
the Charter will remain defective and unfulfilled. The Parliament of Canada must quickly follow the lead taken by Ontario and British Columbia so that property rights are no longer to be excluded from our Constitution.

Mr. Speaker, historians will label 1986 as the year of "Mulrogates". People will remember 1986 as the year of the famous $2 million loan of the former Minister of Regional Industrial Expansion and the case of the Member for Gamelin.
But the spotlight was on the Prime Minister (Mr. Mul-roney), with the many scandals which occured throughout the year. In February the Prime Minister attended a summit and made an official visit to France with a retinue of 60 people at $66,000 a night. With 70 other people trailing him, the Prime Minister then went on a tour of Asia which cost in excess of $50,000 a night.
In October, in New York with 24 followers, expenses were $15,000 a night, not to mention $11,000 for limousines. On a trip through western Canada the Prime Minister was accompanied by a planeload of technical gadgets used to record his image for posterity.
The Prime Minister made sure the Americans would be duly impressed by having our Washington embassy publish a 16-page brochure which has no fewer than 17 pictures of the Prime Minister.
A few days ago we learned that the Prime Minister insisted that his nicest cutlery be used during President Reagan's visit to Quebec City in March 1985, for a total tab of $2.6 million.
Finally, Mr. Speaker, the auditor of the Prime Minister, the best Canadian consumer, told us that, for $41 million, the PM had transferred a prison to his own riding.

December 18, 1986

Mr. Speaker, I would like to draw the attention of the House today to the fact that The Financial Post, in "Outlook 87", winter edition 1986-87, gives 111 pages of very positive information about Canada. Under the present Government, Canada is now ranked sixth among major industrialized countries for its economic performance, while it ranked eleventh when the Liberals were in power.
Some very specific statistics included in this magazine indicate an increase of more than $500 billion in GNP for 1986. Salaries paid in 1986 will exceed $270 billion. We have gradually been able to control this country's deficit, since 1984. We have brought interest rates down by 4 per cent, while the unemployment rate has gone down from 11.3 to 9.7 per cent, which means 600 000 jobs more.
These are objective figures, offered to Canadians by Maclean-Hunter Publications, and I must say their editor, Mr. Nankivell, has done a very good job.
I think that during the holiday season, every Member of this House who believes in private enterprise has a duty to bring this message of success to all Canadians.

Mr. Speaker, I am glad to see that the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Clark) is in the House. In my statement, and on behalf of a great many other MPs in the House, I would like to urge the Minister to keep open the embassies which he recently announced would be closed.
The Minister will recall that when the Liberals were in power and they closed the embassy in Quito the Conservatives as well as ourselves protested vigorously. If one speaks to any of the people in External Affairs one will hear them say that that was a great mistake, which is what the Conservatives said at the time. The embassy was re-opened several years later, and the Government now intends to close it again.
It is important for us to have representation in Quito. It is also obvious that we should have a mission in Helsinki which provides a bridge between the East and West in that part of Europe, and particularly in view of the fact that Canada is planning to join with other Nordic nations in greater cooperation for the demilitarization of the Arctic. I urge the Minister to rethink these decisions.

Mr. Speaker, the rate of absenteeism within Canada Post is a national disgrace. The Marchment Report stated that comparisons with the U.S. Postal Service indicate that Canada Post employees consume roughly twice as much sickness and injury leave as do their U.S. counterparts. This information only reinforces the popular stereotype of postal employees.
The stated goal of Canada Post is to reduce annual absenteeism from its present level of over 16 days per employee to 12 days. Why should absenteeism of 12 days per year be acceptable for postal employees when the average for all sectors of the Canadian economy is only six days? It is obvious that most if not all of Canada Post's deficit comes from this incredible absenteeism and its attendant costs. It is time Canada Post stopped two-bitting Canadians to death and instead faced up to this very real problem.

Mr. Speaker, my question is directed to the Minister of Finance. In answer to a question I asked the Minister yesterday about equalization payments to the provinces, the Minister informed the House
December 18, 1986

that he did not promise to provide an extra $175 million annually for equalization.
Mr. Speaker, I checked all the reports published after the press conference given by the Minister in Edmonton in early November, and all the press reports mention the promise made by the Minister of Finance.
In the circumstances, and also considering that the Minister has now had twenty-four hours to reflect on the matter, will he admit that he and his Department promised to pay an extra $175 million annually to the provinces for equalization, and will he now keep this promise and send this money to the provinces?
No, Mr. Speaker.

Mr. Speaker, yesterday, the Minister challenged us, saying that if we could prove that he had made this promise, he would resign.
Mr. Speaker, the press reports contain a number of articles under the following headlines, and I quote the Minister of Finance:

The Minister of Finance said to Matthew Fisher of The Globe and Mail: "We offered $175 million a year in enhancement, or almost $1 billion over the next five years". Does the Minister of Finance recognize that in fact he made that promise to give the money to the provinces?

Mr. Speaker, I have gone further than the Hon. Member. I checked the transcript, not what The Globe and Mail said I said. I checked what I said in the transcript and the answer is still no, I did not promise.

subtopic: UNEMPLOYMENT INSURANCE ACT, 1971 MEASURE TO AMEND

speechtext: The House resumed from Wednesday, October 19, consideration of the motion of Mr. Bouchard that Bill C-16, an Act to amend the Unemployment Insurance Act, 1971, be read the second time and referred to a legislative committee.

December 18, 1986
Unemployment Insurance Act, 1971

subtopic: UNEMPLOYMENT INSURANCE ACT, 1971 MEASURE TO AMEND
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would like to make a few remarks about Bill C-16, an Act to amend the Unemployment Insurance Act to provide for the extension of the variable entrance requirements and to freeze the premiums payed by employers and employees into the Unemployment Insurance fund.
It is unfortunate that the Government has brought this Bill in at this late moment. Here we are in the dying hours of a sitting which will be finished by the end of December. If this Bill is not passed we would revert to a variable entrance requirement and the unemployed would need 14 weeks to qualify for unemployment insurance benefits.
We on this side of the House have no difficulty with supporting the Bill. There is no question that we support it and want it passed as quickly as possible. However, I think we ought to take this opportunity to reflect on the unemployment insurance program because the variable entrance requirement in itself is attached to the regional extended benefits.
The Government recently received the Forget Report in which we find some disturbing recommendations indeed. May I remind the House that when the Forget Commission was set up to look at the unemployment insurance program it was in an atmosphere of deficit cutting. In November of 1984 the Government was all set to cut deficits here, there and everywhere. It tried it through deindexing old age pensions and came up a cropper on that one. The Government made some announcements with respect to unemployment insurance. One was the consideration of pension income as earned income. Another was looking at severence pay and holiday pay as earned income and to appropriately cut back unemployment insurance benefits for those who received either, or for those who took an early retirement and received a pension. Because of the public outcry against that type of mindless cutting the Government set up the Forget Commission.
The Forget Commission was not set up to make the unemployment insurance program more humane, more sensitive or more responsive to the needs of the unemployed. It was set up in direct response to the Government's need and wish to cut $3 billion from the unemployment insurance fund. Magically, as if by osmosis, the Forget Report came back with a report which suggests exactly that. It recommends the removal of $3 billion from the unemployment insurance fund.
It is interesting to speculate on the Forget Commission report. First, it cost $5.2 million, which money came out of the unemployment insurance fund. It did not come out of the general revenues of the Government. Thus employers and employees have paid for this study. The money did not come from the government unemployment insurance accounts. It did not come from the government side of the account; it came from the premium account. It came out of the contributions of employers and employees. The Chairman of the commission was paid $725 per day plus $125 per day expenses. I am always amazed at how the rich and well-heeled can sit back
and make recommendations regarding the levels of income that poor people receive. If we had some time I would like to do some speculation on that subject. However, I wish to take a look at what was said in the Forget Commission report.
Mr. Forget said that he went across the country and listened to Canadians. In fact, he received 475 briefs, most of which came from trade unions, individuals and advocacy groups. About 19 per cent of the briefs came from the business sector. In addition, the Forget Commission received 1,500 written briefs along with which there were no appearances. Mr. Forget said that he listened and that there were a great many complaints and much criticism that the unemployment insurance fund was unfair, unjust and that it was abused.
I have examined the briefs. I have found that a very small number of them, primarily the ones from the Canadian Chamber of Commerce and the federation of small business- just two or three briefs-recommended the type of Draconian measures that Mr. Forget and the majority of his commission recommended. For example, none of the briefs from fishermen recommended the elimination of fishermen's benefits. Only two or three briefs out of the 1,500 recommended the elimination of the regional extended benefits. None of them proposed any annualization. So to whom was Mr. Forget and the majority of his commission tuned in?
In an article which appears in today's The Toronto Star Mr. Roy Bennett points out that the commission report states the following:
To address the question of fairness, it is important to identify those income groups that are the chief beneficiaries of unemployment insurance and the $3 billion of regional extended benefits.
He goes on to state that the unemployment insurance program was not redistributing wealth adequately. That is not what the unemployment insurance program is designed to do. No reputable individual who I know has suggested that the function of the unemployment insurance program is to redistribute wealth. The program was established to insure against the loss of income as a result of becoming unemployed. That is what the unemployment insurance program was designed to do.
It seems to me that Governments of the past have recognized that in some parts of the country the chances of becoming unemployed are much greater than in other parts of the country. For example, in the Golden Horseshoe at this point in time a person can leave one job and walk into another tomorrow. That is not uncommon. We must also recognize that in other parts of the country the same thing is not so easy. In fact, there are parts of the country where it is important to Canada's economic health that the resources be mined, fished and cut. We must recognize that those are seasonal operations. Thus we insure workers against the loss of income should they lose their jobs. That is the underpinning of the unemployment insurance program.
Mr. Forget has come along and said in his very wealthy, blithe and autocratic way that we can eliminate the regional extended benefits and we can annualize the income of those

collecting UI. In this way a person in Toronto, for example, who has worked 20 weeks will receive $240 a week under the present unemployment insurance system. On the proposal of Mr. Forget another person in St. John's, Newfoundland under the same circumstances with the same insured income will receive $102 a week. He throws in that an earnings supplementation program can be provided. However, when we open the Forget Commission report and try to find details with respect to that program we are forced to ask the following questions. Will it be income-attached? Will it be total family income or individual income? Does one have to be working to collect it? How long will it last? How much will one receive? There are no details with respect to these questions. However, there are all sorts of details with respect to what will be cut off and how it will be cut off, but nothing with respect to what will replace it. Canadians right across the country are not prepared to accept that pig-in-a-poke approach-no way!

PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS-MOTIONS   CONSTITUTION ACTS, 1867-1982 SUGGESTED AMENDMENT TO ABOLISH SENATE
speechtext:
That, in the opinion of this House, the Constitution Acts, 1867 to 1982, should be amended in order to abolish the Senate, and that this House urges that the Senate and the Legislative Assemblies of all provinces pass similar resolutions, and that the Governor General issue a Proclamation under the Great Seal of Canada to that effect.
He said: Mr. Speaker, it is with pleasure, perhaps tinged with regret that this motion is no longer a votable item, that I rise today to present this motion and to say that I am proud and happy that it is very much in the mainstream tradition of my Party. When I first came to this House, given some of the statements made during the 1984 election campaign and repeated in the House since that time, with the notable exception of the decimated remnants of the former Liberal Government, I was hopeful that, while this motion might not lead to the abolition of the Senate and the arrival of the moving vans tomorrow or even next week, it would indeed assist in setting in motion the processes required to rid this country of an institution which was once an embellishment but is now an embarrassment.
Today I would like to acknowledge the record of members of my Party, some of whom are no longer in this House, who have proposed and argued for the abolition of the Senate. I would like to acknowledge the contribution of former Leaders of this Party and its precursors and predecessors. I would also like to
The Senate
acknowledge the contribution of the Leader of my Party, the Hon. Member for Oshawa (Mr. Broadbent). It was he who introduced a motion in the House on March 11, 1985. Rather than quote the complete motion, I would instance a couple of its clauses:
Whereas the Senate of Canada enjoys legislative powers, but exercises these powers without popular mandate;
Whereas the Senate of Canada is a product of an earlier period when democracy had not yet matured in Canada;
Whereas adoption of this resolution would continue to allow for the creation of new and democratic legislative institutions by the Government of Canada and the provinces of Canada;
This House urges the Government of Canada and the Governments of the provinces to act as expeditiously as possible to abolish the Senate of Canada.
At that time, surprisingly enough, members of the Official Opposition gave their consent to the debate of such a motion. Unfortunately, the Government, through a speech from the now Minister of Justice (Mr. Hnatyshyn) along the lines of the need for consultation and consensus, essentially turned down that initiative. Thus, I believe, the Government missed a great opportunity to rid Canadian society and the Parliament of Canada of an anachronism.
I shall quote again from the motion of my Hon. Leader:
Whereas the Senate of Canada enjoys legislative powers, but exercises these powers without popular mandate;
If I were to make a one-sentence summary of my case for the abolition of the Senate, those are the words I would use. The Senate of Canada operates within the Canadian parliamentary framework without a popular mandate.
I would like to refresh the memory of the House of the exchange which took place in March 1985 between the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) and the Leader of the Official Opposition The Prime Minister, tongue in cheek and ever quick, offered the Leader of the Official Opposition the chance to bring in a motion to abolish the Senate if it was supported by the Liberal Party. Unfortunately, the Leader of the Opposition chose not to call the Prime Minister's bluff. Had he done so, he might have either embarrassed the Government or, indeed, forced it to act on the offer that was made rather than merely relying on rhetoric, wit and evasion to accomplish their objectives within the parliamentary process.
I do not wish to provide an historical survey today; indeed, time does not allow. Nor do I want to deal with personalties. There must be rules of mutual respect. While the Senate continues to exist, I will do my best to observe it. Although it is difficult to deal with either assembly without referring to individuals and practices, I am sure you will correct me if I err on this rule, Mr. Speaker.
In the context of the resolution, it matters little what the personal work or merits, opinions, strengths or weaknesses, habits, shortcomings, real, imagined or alleged are of the Members of the other House. Indeed, it matters not very much what the level of their income from their official duties, if I could use the term ever so loosely, might be. It matters little what income they draw from other sources, whether it be

December 18, 1986
The Senate
simply Old Age Security pensions or directors' fees and residual incomes such as in some cases is said to amount to hundreds of thousands of dollars. In trying to avoid the ad hominem or ad feminem arguments, I would have to ask for the forebearance of the House because it very difficult indeed to ignore some of the grosser examples that have been presented to us from time to time.
I would like to discuss briefly the background of second chambers in general. In western constitutional history, bicameralism was originally justified by the need to represent the aristocratic element of society in a distinctive and powerful way within Parliament. The classical theory was expressed by Montesquieu in his The Spirit of Laws. Second chambers, however, have indeed been passionately decried. The objection of Sieyes in the French Revolution is well known: if it contradicts the popular chamber, then it is not democratic; if it merely agrees, then of course it is unnecessary.
To quote a Canadian context, a Father of Confederation, Georges-Etienne Cartier, claimed that the Senate provided the power of resistance to oppose the democratic element. Indeed, today there is still on the walls of that chamber the quote from Cicero: "It is the duty of the nobles to oppose the fickleness of the multitudes".
Harold Laskey, the British political scientist, said that anyone who examines the nature and history of second chambers in general will discover that their main purpose is at least to delay and, if possible, to prevent the disturbance of the status quo. They are, in fact, conservative structures, using that term in its small "c" sense. I am glad to know that many of my colleagues within the Progressive Conservative Party believe that the Senate has outlived its usefulness.
Since World War II, there has been a trend away from bicameralism throughout the world. Second chambers have been abolished in Denmark and Sweden, and in 1968 the Province of Quebec finally rid itself of the last provincial second chamber in Canada. According to a survey carried out in the last decade, a single elected chamber prevails in 84 countries and bicameralism in only 55.
The faults of the institution derive from the fact that the Senate was established during an immature phase of Canadian democracy. I do not claim that the present phase is perfect but it has at least matured in its institutions. The Senate was modelled, as are so many of our institutions, on the British constitutional model; in this case, the House of Lords. It was to replicate the function the House of Lords served at a time when Canada functioned very much as an appendage of the United Kingdom.
Canada's system was modelled on the British House of Lords where the principle was, though not explicitly stated, to provide a brake for the powerful, the privileged and the landed interests on the initiatives of the democratic society. Second chambers were considered necessary to protect business and commercial interests from the irresponsible operations of popular Government.
The Senate is neither regionally representative today, nor is it democratic. It is, to quote Bob Rae, an undemocratic institution working at the heart of a democratic Government. I would like to quote from an editorial which appeared in the local newspaper. I found it to be very persuasive on the subject. It said:
As a body of provincial representation, it is obsolete-overtaken by the elaborate institutionalization of federal-provincial relations... The first ministers' conference has become a permanent feature of the political system. Premiers can press their provincial interests more powerfully, and more legitimately, than any senator.
The Member for Kamloops-Shuswap (Mr. Riis) referred to the Senate as a home of hacks, flacks, and bagmen. Such it is, and as such it can cost an average in projected terms of $1.5 million to keep a Senator there until retirement. Younger Senators, of course, are more expensive. But I think the worst demonstration of misuse of the appointment power to the Senate has to be that started under the Trudeau regime of using it as a holding tank for campaign teams.
Around 90 per cent or more of the legislation that determines the way in which we live our lives in Canada comes from unicameral institutions, Indian bands, municipal governments, provinces, and school boards. Why do we need a Senate today? We do not.

subtopic: PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS-MOTIONS   CONSTITUTION ACTS, 1867-1982 SUGGESTED AMENDMENT TO ABOLISH SENATE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would support the Hon. Member's motion if only he had provided for the immediate replacement of an appointed Senate by an elected body following its abolition.

The last time I rose in this House to speak about the reform of the Senate was during the debate on my own motion which asked for a reform of the second Chamber. This was on May 17, 1985. Since then, an increasing number of Canadians have expressed their support for a reform of this unfortunately outdated institution. Some say that we are wasting time speaking about it. I disagree.

I would agree that we have not yet developed the critical mass required to provoke reform. By discussing today the need to reform the other place, we are adding our voices to the momentum for reform.
I firmly believe that the concept of Senate reform has momentum. More people are talking about it, and more seriously. I hear Senators talking about it. I read Senate reform policies adopted by distinguished political parties. University students are writing papers and theses on the need and alternatives for reform.
One of the most forceful and persuasive statements on the need for Senate reform was made on the Hill 10 days ago by the distinguished former Premier of the Province of Alberta, who was not always known for his endorsement of such an institution. Indeed, Mr. Lougheed confessed to his conversion
December 18, 1986

to the course of an elected, effective, and equal Senate having examined the distinguished report on that subject which was done by a select committee of his own legislature. He went on to indicate that many in western Canada and Atlantic Canada, and some in central Canada, are coming to the view that one of the institutions which would need to be reformed in order to hold together this rather desparate nation would be the institution of a triple-E Senate.
I would contend that the discussions about reform have crystalized around two central notions. First, the need to give the Senate legitimacy by electing its members; second, the importance of making representation in the Senate equal for each province.
Some people unfairly and inaccurately portray the Senate as a do-nothing institution. Senators are portrayed as lay-about political hacks, as my hon. friend has suggested. Neither assertion remotely resembles the truth. The truth is that the Senate is populated by some of Canada's brightest and hardest working people. Much of the work the Senate accomplishes is unsung, unseen, and yet invaluable. I am thinking particularly of the pre-study of legislation. The pre-study work of the Senate's committees is not recorded anywhere, and it is not well known. Nonetheless, it has done much to make our laws clear and workable.

No, Mr. Speaker, I do not urge a reform of the Senate because of any lack of respect for the work done by our senators. Far from it!

I favour reform in order to give legitimacy to the good work done in the other place. The only way that the Senate can gain legitimacy is if its members are elected. Many, perhaps even most Senators, agree with me on this point.
It is essential that we define our expectations and intentions for a reformed Senate. I favour the triple-E Senate with equal representation from each province. I conceive of a reformed Senate as achieving the purpose originally ascribed to it by the Fathers of Confederation: that of a regional counterweight within the national legislature, to balance the more populace regions in matters of federal jurisdiction.
This is a federation with jurisdiction divided between two orders of government. The objective of Senate reform is to restore regional and sectional balance to the debates in matters of federal jurisdiction, not to give the provincial governments a foot in the door of the federal legislature. That would betray the very concept of a federation.
Numerous reports, position papers, and government Bills were tabled, discussed, and introduced during the Liberals' long reign under Mr. Trudeau. However, as documented by Mr. Bill Yurko, a former Member of Parliament, not one of these government initiatives or Liberal dominated committees from 1972 to 1983 supported an elected Senate. Indeed, the only Liberal dominated report to support election to the other
The Senate
place was the report of the Special Committee on Senate Reform of 1984. It is interesting and important to note that in his discussion paper presented to the committee the then Justice Minister, the Hon. Mark MacGuigan, stated:
The Government of Canada has no set position on how the Senators should be chosen.
His discussion paper neither recommended nor rejected an elected Senate. That was the Liberal Party's position in 1984. I am afraid that the Liberals are Johnny-come-latelies to the idea of a democratic second chamber. In fact, it has been pointed out that at their recent policy conference which was so successful in one of its objectives, but so great a failure in its attempt to formulate any policy, another resolution was adopted which would, if it became law, render such a Senate virtually impossible. The Liberal Party endorsed a constitutional amendment that would in effect give both Quebec and Ontario a veto over future constitutional amendments. That, I submit, would forestall such a development.
With all respect, I do hope that this particular motion will fire some genuine and sincere debate. I applaud the Hon. Member for reintroducing the subject into the Chamber. The time has come for a serious debate and serious action on this matter.
Before commenting on the Hon. Member's Party and its position, I would like to say one final thing about the Official Opposition's position on the issue. In my opinion, there is some doubt about the sincerity of the position adopted by the Liberal Party on Grey Cup weekend. It is a well named weekend, by the way, since most of the material coming out of the Congress Centre was grey in colour. I would suggest that when the Bill by the Hon. Member for Bow River (Mr. Taylor) was talked out the other day in the Chamber, it was talked out by representatives of the Liberal Party. I submit that that shows their lack of seriousness about the issue.
In contrast, we can at least say this for the New Democrats. Their stance on the Senate has been consistent, albeit consistently wrong. Still today we have an hon. gentleman, a member of the New Democratic Party, proposing the abolition of the Senate. That would deny a fundamental and still relevant aspect of the Confederation agreement. I suggest it will fall on barren ground, at least in western Canada.
Two aspects of the Confederation agreement as forged at Charlottetown and Quebec City are regularly underemphasized. First, that Confederation was and is in great part an economic arrangement. How the economic costs and benefits of nationhood were to be distributed was a primary focus of the discussion which led to Confederation, and an essential aspect of the agreement.

Second, the Fathers of Confederation, and there were unfortunately no mothers of Confederation, were very concerned about the role and status of the second House of the Federal Parliament. They spent more time discussing the

December 18, 1986
The Senate
Senate than the division of powers. That is an historical fact, Mr. Speaker.

I mention these two facts because they are linked. I am convinced that if Canada's regions are to share equally in the nation's prosperity, as is their due under the Confederation agreement, our national institutions must be strengthened. The most important of these is the Senate, for an objective consideration of the proceedings of the Chalottetown and Quebec conferences and of the proceedings of the various legislatures leads to the definitive conclusion that the Senate was intended as the principal voice of regional and sectional interests in matters of federal jurisdiction. History proves that neither Cabinet nor the provinces can guarantee economic justice within Confederation. That job is properly assigned to the Senate. The Fathers of Confederation knew that. We just have to live up to their intent.

Mr. Speaker, I had not meant to make a partisan speech today, at least not unduly. However, it will be very difficult to restrain myself as much as I would like after hearing the ridiculous comments about the Liberal Party by the Hon. Member who represents the ridiculous Conservative Party.
In his not so eloquent remarks, the Hon. Member made some reference to the fact that it was the fault of the Liberals the other day that a motion in the House did not proceed. He said that the Liberals talked it out. That is fascinating. As I recall the situation, there were exactly the same number of speakers from each Party, all of whom spoke for the maximum 10 minutes. This leads me to believe that each Member who spoke deliberately used his or her time. Therefore, Conservative Members are just as responsible as anyone else for the motion not proceeding. I ask the Hon. Member across the way what kind of moral honesty is that? If I were he, I would fire that speech writer immediately. Any speech writer who cannot give an Hon. Member better information than that does not deserve his or her paycheque.
The Tories can never speak for themselves. They are the silent majority in the House. They are the book-ends. They are the people who came in with the tide and will go out with the ebb-tide. Those surfers who were elected in the last election should perhaps think about that before making such ridiculous remarks in the House of Commons.
The subject at hand is very important and should not be a partisan issue. Of course that is the last thing I would want to do. The Hon. Member for Kenora-Rainy River (Mr. Parry) proposed a motion today that we should amend the Constitution of the country to abolish the Senate. Of course that really means that we should abolish one of the two Chambers of Parliament. Let us not forget that the two Houses of Parliament are sovereign. Therefore, any remark to the effect that we should abolish or dissolve half of our parliamentary institution is extremely inappropriate.
I say to Hon. Members of the Democratic Party that there are reasons for the existence of that institution. The Hon. Member for Kenora-Rainy River may have referred to some of them, but unfortunately he forget to mention that which works well in the Senate. As well, he completely forgot that there were reasons for the establishment of the Senate other than the unique one to which he referred. In part he referred to the fact that the Senate was appointed in an era in which the democratically elected House of Commons was viewed as somewhat immature. That may have been one of the reasons at that time, but there was also another one.
The Hon. Member is a student of history. He must know the history of Canada. When Canada East and Canada West, formerly Upper and Lower Canada, and the two Atlantic provinces joined together in 1867, there was an agreement that proportional representation would be given to one House and that there would be a guarantee in the other House ensuring that the regions of the country were represented. Perhaps he forgot that part of the equation. However, he should remember it, especially since the Members of the New Democratic Party purportedly speak to matters important to everyone, in a sanctimonious way. They should remember that, especially having consulted with their Quebec caucus chairman as they must have done earlier this week.
The original arrangement was to have in Canada a Senate with a third of its representation from the Province of Quebec, a third from the Province of Ontario, and a third from the maritime provinces. In that formula there was a constitutional guarantee to provide a minimum number of seats for the Province of Quebec.

And the Hon. Member is of course aware that at the time, people felt it was important for the Fathers of Confederation to have a mechanism that would ensure that the linguistic duality of our country would always be reflected in the Parliament of Canada. Earlier this week, when we were having a similar debate in the House, I mentioned that after the 1979 election campaign, when the Clark Government headed by the present Secretary of State for External Affairs was elected, its leader had to go to the Senate to get someone to represent this province in his Government. And I am not being partisan, since he doesn't even belong to my party.
My point is that it was important for this particular Prime Minister, and perhaps for others in the future, to be able to seek out representatives from certain regions in our country to ensure that those regions, and especially when we're talking about Quebec... There is a particular concern here because when we are talking about Quebec, we are talking about one of the two founding peoples. In the Clark Government, one of the two was not even represented in the Government, not because of the Prime Minister but because only one Member had been elected in that province. Only two Members, but only one Francophone. And so he did not have enough Members to appoint as Ministers in his Cabinet. And that is when he opted for going to the Senate, and I think that was an inspired
December 18, 1986

gesture. What would the Hon. Member who is proposing to abolish the Senate have done in that kind of situation?
Does he mean that if one of the two founding peoples had not managed to elect Members on the Government side, they would not deserve to be represented in that Government? Is that what the New Democrats are trying to say today? I wonder whether that is what they really want. If that is the NDP position, then the House and the entire country ought to know, because for a long time we have been hearing about this so-called NDP formula for parliamentary modernization, which includes abolishing one of the two Houses of our Parliament, and thus potentially preventing one of the two founding peoples from getting the kind of recognition it has received in the past. And that is not mere speculation, Mr. Speaker, since it actually happened in the last ten or twenty years.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to make just a few remarks. Perhaps I could clear up something which was the object of controversy between the Hon. Member for Glengarry-Prescott-Russell (Mr. Boudria) and the Hon. Member for Edmonton South (Mr. Edwards) in respect of the Private Member's Bill of the Hon. Member for Bow River (Mr. Taylor) regarding the creation of an elected Senate. He was quite mistaken to imagine that anyone talked that Bill out. It was selected as a votable item and there are at least four hours of debate left. You could not talk that Bill out if you wanted to because it has to come to a vote. That was one of the more meaningless debates we have had around here in a long time, with the Liberals and Conservatives trying to figure out who talked out a Bill which procedurally cannot be talked out. I suppose that is par for the course in some respects.
As to abolition of the Senate, the Hon. Member for Kenora-Rainy River (Mr. Parry) said that is the traditional NDP position. I regard that as the preferable option. The best thing we could do would be to abolish the Senate. However, I have no illusions about the possibility of that coming to be the political consensus. In western Canada a consensus is building for another kind of change to the Senate, that is for an elected Senate. We will have plenty of opportunity to consider this issue as a result of the Hon. Member for Bow River's motion and it will be interesting to see what people say and how they vote on the motion. I think it is one of the more interesting issues to be put to a vote as a result of the new procedure on Private Members' Business. I am kind of excited by the possibilities and how it will turn out. However, when we are thinking about reform, let us not just think about the Senate, let us also think about the House of Commons.
One of the primary concerns about the Senate has been whether or not it lives up to its original function of representing the regions. Does it address the problem, as seen by many Canadians, of the political process being dominated by the interests of Quebec and Ontario? But let us ask ourselves not only what Senate reform might do in that respect but also what House of Commons reform might do.
I ask Members to think about proposals for some combination of proportional representation in the House of Commons alongside the kind of representation we have now. I personally would not be in favour of going to full proportional representation along the lines of the Israeli system, for example, where party lists are the only way people get into the Chamber, and where there is none of what we regard as a traditional parliamentary system in which people represent identifiable

December 18, 1986
The Senate
areas and constituents. However, West Germany has a system where a certain number, I believe it is two-thirds, of their members are elected in the traditional parliamentary way and the other third elected according to proportional representation. If we were to adopt some Canadian combination of that system here, it might also address the feeling of people in western Canada, for example, that they are not well represented at the centre of the political process. I believe that is behind, to a great degree, the call for Senate reform in western Canada.
The traditional NDP call for abolition is based on the fact that it is not a democratic institution. That objection remains. However, there is a second question as to what we will do to address the feeling that smaller provinces and less powerful regions do not have enough political clout at the centre. I think that can be rectified in a number of ways and that is why I am personally open to the idea of an elected Senate.
I have to say in all honesty that a lot of expectations are being raised about what an elected Senate could do. I cannot imagine it living up to those expectations. There would have to be a great transfer of power from what we normally consider the domain of the House of Commons to an elected Senate, and that would inevitably be much more controversial than those who advocate an elected Senate think it would be. I am not saying that as a criticism, I just think this idea is in its political infancy. It has not been thought through.
For example, a lot of people in western Canada have said recently, in response to the CF-18 decision, that that is all the more evidence of the need for an elected Senate. I have asked myself a number of times how an elected Senate would have prevented that decision. In the end it was a government decision, not a decision of a particular Chamber. In order for those kinds of decisions to be made more fairly through an elected Senate, much more would have to be said about what the relationship between an elected Senate and government decisions would be. That has not been articulated by many of the people who have spoken in favour of an elected Senate. It has not been thought through.
But I did not rise today to criticize that idea. I am certainly open to suggestions for Senate reform which would make it democratic and make it address that sense of regional alienation which exists in certain parts of Canada. I simply caution Members not to create false expectations about how simple it might be to achieve an elected Senate. I imagine it would be very difficult indeed.
As I said at the beginning, we are going to have at least four more hours to debate the issue. As I understand it, the motion put forward by the Hon. Member for Bow River has only been debated for an hour. We will hear from at least 24 or 25 more Members of the House of Commons and then have a vote. It could be a historic vote. If Members of the House of Commons decide by a majority vote to send a message to the Government that they want Senate reform to be taken so seriously that they actually voted for an elected Senate, then that will have been an incredible day for Private Members' Business. It will have
been the result of an initiative of one Private Member along with others. The Hon. Member for Kenora-Rainy River would have had a votable motion on the same issue had the last session not been prorogued and new votable items selected by the committee. I commend both he and the Hon. Member for Bow River and everyone else who is trying to contribute constructively to a debate about the kind of reform we need to address some serious questions of regional alienation, how to make our institutions more democratic, and how to finally get rid of this undemocratic cell within the larger democratic organism.

subtopic: PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS-MOTIONS   CONSTITUTION ACTS, 1867-1982 SUGGESTED AMENDMENT TO ABOLISH SENATE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on October 1, 1986, when the Hon. Member for Kenora-Rainy River (Mr. Parry) presented his motion to abolish the Senate, I am sure he did so without any partisan motives, just as his comments a few minutes ago before the House were equally devoid of such considerations. My Conservative colleague, the Hon. Member for Edmonton South (Mr. Edwards) also made some nonpartisan remarks on this very important subject. It is unfortunate, Mr. Speaker, that the Liberal Member for Glengarry- Prescott-Russell (Mr. Boudria) found it necessary to make comments that smacked of electioneering and petty politics.
I think that when we are discussing subjects of historical or national importance, Members should be a little less flamboyant in their speeches and should, if only for a short while, relax their ideological and political stance. I shall try to follow the example of my colleagues who just spoke and add my own equally non-partisan considerations. First of all, I would like to look at how the issue has evolved during the last fifteen years.
This is not the first time we are talking about changing the Senate. In 1972, a Special Joint Committee on the Constitution spoke out on the role of the Senate. It said that the Senate's principal role was to protect the provinces, minorities and regional interests. The Committee would let the Senate amend certain types of legislation and considered the Senate as the Chamber for sober second thought, away from the political ambience of the legislative process.
The next step was 1978 when the British Columbia Government appointed a committee on the reform of the Canadian Senate. Although the committee did not advocate outright abolition of the institution, they did recommend basic changes. In a nutshell, our friends in British Columbia wanted a reform under which provincial and regional participation would be institutionalized and they suggested that, up to a point, the Senate should be empowered to review legislation. The same year, 1978, an Ontario legislative committee, the Canada West Foundation and a Conservative Party committee seemed to favour the establishment of some kind of a House of the provinces to which provincial MLAs would automatically belong. In other words, MLAs would make up a strong provincial delegation.
In 1979 the Pepin-Robarts Commission came out in favour of a Council of the Federation made up of elected members of
December 18, 1986

various provincial cabinets. These elected members would have the right to vote in the Council of the Federation, which would also include elected federal government representatives who would be entitled to act as such and take part in debates, but without voting rights.
In 1980 the Quebec Liberal Party constitutional committee supported the abolition of the Senate, to be replaced by a federal council which would accept representations from official delegates of the various provincial administrations in this country.
In 1981, once again, we hear from the Canada West Foundation, this time about an elected Senate. In 1982, the Alberta Government, of which my colleague for Edmonton South (Mr. Edwards), who has already spoken on this subject today, used to be a member, proposed that the members of the Senate be appointed by the provincial Governments. This would have given a lot of power to each province over its own representatives.
If I may open a parenthesis, Mr. Speaker, it was also in 1982 that the Quebec Liberals, as I see that my colleague for Glengarry-Prescott-Russell (Mr. Boudria) is back in the House, forced 6 million Quebecers to go down on their knees and sign a Constitution to which they were not a party. I wanted to mention this fact because it is important. This antagonism toward Quebec has created very difficult climates in that province. This week again, the Hon. Member for Notre-Dame-de-Graces (Mr. Allmand), a Liberal, showed his animosity toward Quebec by calling the members of the Societe Saint-Jean-Baptiste du Quebec extremists.
The climate was the same in 1982. It is useful to recall the climate in which the Liberals had us live for many years.
In 1984, Mr. Speaker, we had a Joint Committee of the Senate and the House of Commons on Senate Reform. This Committee proposed that members of the Senate be elected by the Canadian people. There would have been compulsory elections for senators. This was much more democratic than the method used by the Liberals to force us, Quebecers, to accept the Constitution in 1982.
Then, more recently, in August 1986, we had the Premiers' Conference in Edmonton which resulted in the Edmonton Statement. At that point, the First Ministers had agreed on a proposal put forward by Quebec's Premier, Mr. Robert Bourassa, which stated Quebec's willingness to sign the Constitution, joining in as a partner. But Quebec's Premier suggested to his colleagues from other provinces that before negotiations could open and the Constitution approved, Quebec's special status should be recognized. I am referring to the provincial Liberals. At the federal level, there is no understanding as yet as to what should be agreed to first among federal Liberals.
Premier Bourassa added that the Province of Quebec should have some authority in immigration matters, in order to increase Quebec's immigration quotas. Finally, Quebec's Premier referred to the vetoing formula, formula 7/75 under
The Senate
which seven provinces or 75 per cent of the population were needed to amend the Constitution. Premier Bourassa stated that three Supreme Court judges should be appointed by Quebec. And, finally, he said there should be a limitation on the Federal Government's spending authority in matters of provincial jurisdiction.
Those are things that may be questionable, Mr. Speaker, but at least they make up the policy of a Government whose Leader is a real Leader. There are no differences of opinion among provincial Liberals on the Constitution. However, there are major differences among federal Liberals on that issue.
Finally, Mr. Speaker, we had the November 1986 First Ministers Conference in Vancouver where the participants agreed to deal with the first stage of a possible amendment process with respect to the Constitution and the Senate, but the points raised by Quebec Premier Bourassa would have to be settled first. They agreed there would be a second stage when the agenda might include the very important issue of potential changes to our Senate, along with statements on property right, fisheries, and a variety of major topics of national interest.
For these reasons, Mr. Speaker, we would be well advised not to proceed any further with the project advocated by my socialist colleague on the other side of the House and to wait until the major recommendations of Mr. Bourassa have been implemented.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I welcome this opportunity to speak to the motion before the House today. I realize the brilliant speech by the Hon. Member for Levis (Mr. Fontaine) will be a difficult act to follow, but I would like to make a few comments just the same.
First of all, Mr. Speaker, I would like to comment on what was said earlier by the Liberal Member, when he said that when in 1979, the then Prime Minister, Mr. Clark, did not have enough Members from Quebec, he went to the Senate to get the representation he needed in his Cabinet for one of the two founding peoples of this country. I think that was an excellent idea, and I'm glad the Hon. Member brought it up. What I did not appreciate, however, is when in 1982, the Senate was a good deal less eager to ensure that the second or rather the first of the two founding peoples had its place within the Canadian Constitution and the repatriation process.
Mr. Speaker, recent events among our neighbours to the south, and I am referring to certain relations with certain countries and the arms sale, I find very perplexing. And I am especially embarrassed when I think of the young people who are watching us. I have been involved in education, and I have always tried to judge what we do as adults in terms of the upcoming generation, the generation that will take our place tomorrow.

December 18, 1986
The Senate
And I thought that this was certainly one of the worst examples one could have given to young people today, and I wondered: What do we really have to offer American or Canadian youth? What are we actually going to offer them as Canadians, when we tell them: Listen, just trust the present generation. Watch what we are doing. We have the solutions, we have the means, and we are going to build a country commensurate with your aspirations.
And just look at the disappointed young people to the south and even in our own country, who are asking: Is that the administration that was supposed to build a better world for tomorrow?
Mr. Speaker, it is a little bit like what is going on in the House. It's nothing to write home about. What is the point in saying that we are the pick of the crop, the highest authority in the land, when we spend endless days arguing about a single figure. This idea about a Senate reform is not new and obviously, it won't be implemented overnight. Mr. Speaker, you are well aware that the young Canadians who are watching us as we deal with the unemployment rate which is going down, but not quickly enough- they are watching us on TV and say: what are they talking about today in the House? We talked about the reform of the Senate, we dealt with such and such point. That is no relevancy between these points and the future we should be building for young people.
The House will remember the unfortunate event in 1985 when the Senate refused to adopt a budgetary legislation to provide the Government with a borrowing authority. The whole financial and business community was wondering what was going to happen. For seven or eight weeks, the Senate refused systematically to adopt this legislation, and some senators of a different party were taunting us saying: Do your homework all over again, for we are the House of sober second thought.
Really, Mr. Speaker, we will have to deal with this problem, not necessarily by abolishing the Senate. We should use all our resources. Considered individually, all these people are a source of hope for young Canadians. On the other hand, the energy and vast resources of these people should be channeled, not after the fact, but during the legislative process, into discussions to which the elected representatives could contribute.
Mr. Speaker, basically, as long as the Senate remains a second Chamber able to block the Bills adopted by the duly elected Members of this House, there will remain a division of political parties and the second Chamber will continue to be a means to postpone the passage of Bills and legislation which a freely elected government is entitled to have implemented, and to my knowledge, there was no take over of power with machine guns in Canada in 1984. This is a question of partisanship, and we can see how clearly the Senate is divided along political lines at this time. It seems to me that we should now go beyond this type of upper Chamber.
For these reasons, Mr. Speaker, I believe that the Senate should be replaced, but we have to decide with what.
