I am sure my colleagues know that interest in Senate reform has been increasing in recent years. A number of reform projects have even been made public, but there is still no consensus as to how we should proceed. There is no need to remind Hon. Members that Senate reform has been the object of many studies.
The best thing I can do today is review some of the major recommendations made in the past few years. I will begin with the report of the Special Joint Committee of the Senate and of
December 18, 1986

the House of Commons on the Constitution of Canada. In its report the committee points out that, at the beginning, the role of the Senate was to protect the interests of provinces, minorities and regions, and to proceed to a review of legislation, the sober second thought. The committee feels that the Senate must be reorganized-not abolished-because the reasons which justified its creation in 1867 are still valid. The committee recommends that the federal Government continue to appoint senators but, as seats become vacant, half the senators be appointed by the federal Government, according to a list of nominees submitted by the provincial or territorial Government involved, the other half being selected the same way as it is today.
Mr. Speaker, in 1978, in a document called Reform of the Canadian Senate, the Government of British Columbia recommended that the Senate should not be abolished but modified. According to this paper, the Senate's principal role should be to institutionalize provincial or regional participation in the federal decision-making process, its secondary role being to examine the Bills adopted by the House of Commons. The paper also recommended that senators should be appointed and released from their duties by the provincial Governments and that the senior senator for each province should be a provincial Minister.
Mr. Speaker, still in 1978, the Ontario Select Committee on Constitutional Reform of the Ontario Legislative Assembly, the Canada West Foundation and the Progressive Conservative Party recommended abolishing the Senate and replacing it with a House of the Provinces. The Ontario Committee proposed that members should be appointed by the provincial governments and represent those governments. Provincial Members, Ministers and the Premier of each province would be eligible.
Mr. Speaker, I see that our speaking time is running out. All the recommendations I have just mentioned-and I have a list of a dozen other recommendations from all parts of Canada- had the same focus, and that is, not abolishing the Senate but replacing it or changing it in some way or other, and doing so within the Canadian Constitution, and after consultation with, and the approval of, all the provinces. Therefore we cannot proceed in the manner suggested by the Hon. Member.

subtopic: PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS-MOTIONS   CONSTITUTION ACTS, 1867-1982 SUGGESTED AMENDMENT TO ABOLISH SENATE
speechtext:
It being 4.30 p.m., pursuant to Order made on Wednesday, December 17, 1986, the House shall now revert to Statements by Ministers.
Statements by Ministers

Mr. Speaker, today I am announcing the policies which will provide new direction for our financial services industry.
Pursuant to the provisions of Standing Order 67(2) I have the honour to lay upon the Table copies, in both official languages, of documents pertaining to regulatory reform in the financial sector.
This is an industry which touches all Canadians. Our savings accounts, mortgages, car loans, insurance policies, all of these and more, are financial products essential to our daily lives, and it is critical that we be well served by this industry. There are few Canadians whose lives are not touched in one way or another every day by a financial institution.
All Hon. Members know that Canada is fortunate to possess one of the finest financial systems in the world. It is composed of sound world class institutions. It employs hundreds of thousands of Canadians and serves millions. It is one of Canada's leading export industries, which is something we ought not to forget. The financial industry is in the midst of rapid change. Communications technology has created 24 hour global markets. The importance of international capital flows has dramatically increased, and the traditional roles of financial institutions are changing. They are now doing far more than they used to.
These global forces, quite frankly, have challenged existing legislation designed for an earlier and less dynamic era. That is why, early in its mandate, the Government announced its intention to work with the provinces, the public and the financial community to reform financial regulations in order to seize the opportunities offered by change.
In April of last year, the Government set out its objectives for financial reform. We made specific proposals to focus the debate. In the 18 months since that time, extensive discussion, study and analysis have taken place and a variety of views have been expressed. First, I find there is a widespread appreciation of the key role of the financial sector in our economic renewal, not just in facilitating investment in Canada, but as an exporter and employer. Second, there is agreement that our financial system is fundamentally sound and that the basic division of supervisory responsibility for our institutions should remain in place.

There is universal acknowledgement of the trend toward integrated financial services, both here and abroad, and broad agreement on the benefits this brings to consumers.

December 18, 1986
Statements by Ministers

There is continuing concern regarding self dealing and abuses of conflict of interest in both closely and widely held institutions. This also has been evident in the last 18 months. We have received detail and practical advice on how to improve our regulatory and supervisory structures. While there have been diverse views expressed on the best means to regulate our financial system, all of us seek the same goal. What we want is a sound financial system which provides Canadians with innovative and competitive services, which broadens the range of choice for Canadian savers and investors and which fosters safe and well supervised financial institutions which can compete effectively around the world.
I am announcing policies today which will achieve these important objectives, policies which we believe are realistic, balanced and, above all, workable. The document I am tabling today is entitled New Directions for the Financial Sector, which will allow the Canadian financial community to plan and act with confidence. It outlines the policies which will be tabled as legislation in 1987. It also provides the framework in which the Government will exercise the specific powers regarding the transfer of ownership as proposed in Bill C-8 and Bill C-9, both of which received first reading on October 6, 1986.
The policies we are proposing are policies for the next generation of financial institutions. They are far ranging and will have a profound and positive impact. They deal with interrelated issues which call for an integrated approach. I believe careful study of the document 1 am tabling today is necessary to gain a full appreciation of the scope of our proposals.
What is the essence of our approach? It is to act in four interrelated areas. First, we will allow the integration of financial services through the common ownership of institutions and the extension of powers. Second, we will introduce a pragmatic ownership policy which checks the growth of commercial financial links in the economy while maintaining balanced competition within the financial services sector. Third, we will provide a strong framework for prudential regulation. Fourth, we will modernize and strengthen our supervisory system.

In short, we will introduce a pragmatic ownership policy, provide a strong framework for prudential regulation. And, modernize and strengthen our supervisory system.

Let me discuss each area in turn. First, with respect to the integration of financial services, the Government believes our laws should reflect today's market reality. The banks and nonbank financial institutions today are not only capable of providing, but are actually providing, an evermore common range of services which meet the needs of all Canadians as savers, borrowers or as investors. In order to foster such common benefits, the Government will end unnecessary institutional barriers within the financial services industry and
will allow the integration of financial services. Restrictions on common ownership of regulated financial institutions will be removed, allowing common ownership through affiliates or subsidiaries. Separate institutions will be maintained for supervisory purposes, but full networking of services will be allowed between institutions, except for the retailing of property and casualty insurance and life insurance.
In-house powers will be broadened for institutions in the various "pillars" of the financial industry. All trust, loan and life insurance companies will be granted full consumer lending powers. The larger of them will be eligible for full commercial lending powers. All federally regulated institutions will be able to offer investment advice and portfolio management services. Banks and insurance companies will be granted ancilliary fiduciary powers. From the point of view of Canadian consumers, these policies will allow your neighbourhood branches to offer a wide array of innovative and convenient services with greater potential for one-stop shopping.
The philosophy underpinning financial services integration would be to build, not to buy. To protect against harmful concentration, acquisition of financial services companies will reaquire the approval of the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson). As a general rule, large financial institutions will not be allowed to acquire other large institutions. An exception to this general policy will be made for the securities industry. Given the desire for a viable Canadian presence in this strategic industry, the federal Government will permit domestically owned, federally regulated financial institutions to build or buy securities dealer subsidiaries. Necessary legislative amendments to permit such participation in the securities industry will be introduced in the near future.
The second area of action is a pragmatic and responsible ownership policy. Current Canadian law requires all large domestic banks to be widely held, and new domestic banks to attain widely-held status within 10 years. Trust, loan and stock insurance companies, on the other hand, do not have similar ownership rules. Many of these institutions also have significant commercial links.
While this variety of ownership forms is not unique to Canada, the development of significant links between these non-bank financial institutions and companies with commercial interests has been a source of intense debate. Some have emphasized the issue of concentration of power.

Some have emphasized the issue of concentration of power and the potential for self-dealing and conflict of interest. However, there is also widespread recognition that entrepreneurial owners have been a source of dynamism in the industry. They have provided firms with the leadership and financial strength to compete with our large banks.
December 18, 1986



One argument is that financial institutions should be widely held. The other argument is that it is also useful to have closely held entrepreneur-oriented financial institutions. Both arguments are valid. As with many issues in this complex age, a balance must be struck.
To lessen the potential dangers of commercial-financial links while promoting competition, the Government intends to implement the following policy. Smaller banks will be permitted to be closely held by domestic investors with no commercial interests. They will be allowed to remain closely held until they attain a capital base of $750 million, a base which will support about $15 billion in assets. Banks that exceed this capital threshold of $750 million will be subject to the following ownership rules.
Shareholders with less than 10 per cent of the shares in any class, or any series of any class, will be permitted to acquire additional shares to a ceiling of 10 per cent. Shareholders with more than 10 per cent of such shares will not be permitted to acquire additional shares in the same class or series. Within five years of reaching the capital threshold at least 35 per cent of the voting shares must be publicly traded and widely held. The penalty for non-compliance will be a constraint on the bank's ability to grow. These measures will ensure that major existing banks remain widely held, and that closely held banks of substantial size move toward wide ownership as new equity is issued.
Ownership policies regarding trust, loan and insurance companies will be complementary, but they will not be identical, reflecting the different histories and circumstances of these institutions. Like many Canadians the Government is concerned with the potential dangers of growing commercial-financial links. Yet we are equally concerned that an overzealous reaction could limit future competition in the financial sector. Therefore we are proposing a policy which arrests the growth of commercial-financial links while maintaining strong sources of innovation and competition in the market-place.
To achieve these twin objectives the following regime will be implemented effective today. Approval for the incorporation of new trust, loan and insurance companies will be restricted to applicants with no significant commercial interests. Commercial interests will not be permitted to acquire or increase significant ownership positions in non-bank institutions having capital in excess of $50 million. Such larger non-bank institutions with commercial links will be required to have at least 35 per cent of their voting shares publicly traded and widely held by December 31, 1991, or within five years of reaching the $50 million capital threshold. Trust, loan and insurance companies with no commercial links and with capital in excess of $750 million will also be required to have at least 35 per cent of their voting shares publicly traded and widely held by December 31, 1991, or within five years of reaching the $750 million capital threshold. Once this threshold is exceeded no shareholder will be able to acquire an ownership position in the
Statements by Ministers
institution in excess of 10 per cent and significant shareholders will not be permitted to increase their ownership positions.
These policies will foster wider ownership of large financial institutions in the future while recognizing the existing positions of current investors. This means that more Canadians can now buy more shares in their financial institutions. Most important, by causing current laws protecting minority shareholders to come into play they will ensure market disclosure, public scrutiny and the presence of strong outside directors.
Protecting the solvency and integrity of institutions requires more than changes in ownership rules, which is most important. We cannot do this simply through changes in ownership rules. No single ownership policy can protect against imprudent management or questionable business practices. What is needed is an effective and vigilant system of self-governance supported by independent and objective directors and an effective supervisory system.
This is why we will do the following. We will limit commercial-financial links. We will provide sufficiently broad minority shareholding to ensure market disclosure and public scrutiny. We will introduce cumulative voting rules for the election of directors to increase their influence and create a stronger framework for prudential regulation. In this strong framework the Government will strictly control self-dealing in all financial institutions. The list of non-arm's length parties will be expanded and made uniform for banks and non-banks. Most asset transactions between such persons will be banned and service transactions will be strictly controlled. Rules will also be introduced to monitor and control transactions between related financial institutions.
Safeguards against abuses of conflict of interest will be introduced as well. Procedures and controls to prevent the flow of insider information between fiduciary and other financial activities will be implemented. Disclosure rules will be strengthened.
In accord with the over-all approach recommended by Mr. Justice Estey, the basic division of responsibilities for ensuring and monitoring the health of institutions this division among the supervisory authority, the directors of the institution and the external auditors will remain in place. A number of proposals, however, will improve directors' supervision of their institutions' operations and strengthen the role of auditors.

All financial institutions will be required to have a minimum of one-third of their directors independent of the institution. These independent directors will be asked to perform additional duties on corporate review committees made up solely of such independent directors.

During the Estey Inquiry, considerable time and effort was taken to study current accounting principles. As Mr. Justice Estey stated, in some cases difficulties were easy to define but

December 18, 1986
Statements by Ministers
solutions were not easy to develop. In line with his recommendations, a number of steps will be taken, in consultation with the accounting profession, to review accounting standards as they apply to financial institutions. As well, measures will be introduced to ensure appropriate communication among auditors, the financial institutions they audit and federal regulators. These measures to improve the framework for effective regulation will ensure Canadians that they can maintain confidence in the integrity of the financial system while enjoying the benefits of dynamic competition.
The fourth major area in which we are acting is to improve and strengthen the supervision of financial institutions. How are we doing that? Consistent with the integration of financial services to which I spoke a few moments ago, the Office of the Inspector General of Banks and the Department of Insurance will be consolidated into a new body to be called the Office of the Superintendent of Financial Institutions. This new office will have full supervisory responsibilities for banks and for non-bank financial institutions.
The Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) will have over-all responsibility for the new office. The Superintendent will be clearly responsible for the administration of statutes, the assessment of solvency and the execution of supervisory actions. Measures will also be introduced to clarify and expand the Superintendent's power to deal effectively with unsound business practices and to deal with financially troubled institutions.
The Government recognizes that the Superintendent requires a full awareness of market trends and developments. The Government will therefore act on Mr. Justice Estey's recommendation to form an advisory committee of technical experts with a broad mandate including a role in the improvement of early-warning systems.
The Government believes that the Canada Deposit Insurance Corporation should remain a separate body. This will allow the retention of private-sector expertise on the CDIC Board of Directors and it will preserve CDIC's established relationship with provincial authorities supervising CDIC-insured provincial institutions. In maintaining the CDIC as a separate agency, the Government will equip it with additional powers. Premium levels will also be revised to eliminate the existing deficit in a timely way.
These are the four key areas where we are acting to provide new direction for the financial sector: the integration of financial services, a pragmatic ownership policy, a modern framework for prudential regulation and an effective federal supervisory structure. These are four interrelated areas which will provide a framework for a sound and competitive financial system today and for the future.
In putting this policy forward, we have been very much helped by the fine work done by the House Standing Committee and to a large measure we have followed it both philosophically and in detail.

Our policies in these areas are pragmatic-rooted in today's market realities. They are practical. They are balanced. They are needed. And they will work.

As the financial services industry enters this new regime, all Canadians will benefit. The ability to provide innovative and competitive financial products including mortgages, investments and loans to all Canadians in all parts of the country will no longer be artificially limited by outmoded laws. However, where necessary, regulation and supervision are being tightened to protect the savings of Canadians.
We have long had reason to be proud of our financial system. Our institutions have served us well. In my opinion, they have served us well because Canadians have had the wisdom to deal with the world as they found it, to fuse the real with the ideal. We believe these policies follow in that pragmatic and responsible tradition.
These proposals will lay a solid foundation for the future. They will help our institutions grow and prosper. They will ensure that Canadians can continue to have confidence in one of the finest financial systems in the world.
Hear, hear!

Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to have this opportunity to respond on behalf of the Official Opposition to the statement made by the Minister of State for Finance (Mr. Hockin). My remarks must necessarily be preliminary as the documents which the Minister tabled and the notes of his speech were made available only two hours ago and will need further study.
Despite the disappointing evidence of the last two years, we expected better of the Government than that with which it has come forward today. After more than two years of stalling, indecision, governing on a case-by-case basis, squandering the taxpayers' money and squandering its huge mandate, surely Canadians had a right to expect more today than another set of proposals or yet another discussion paper.
If today is a step forward, as the Minister has said, it is a very timid step. There has been a Green Paper. The Government is awash in studies. There have been umpteen promises of the Government's intention to proceed to legislation. After all the fanfare, today we have not a Bill, not actual proposed legislation but a statement of intent.
This is more than just disappointing. It is verging on negligence or on the dereliction of duty. Canadians elected this Government to govern, to show leadership and to tackle the tough issues facing Canada. There are plenty of difficult questions, complex issues and competing interests in the
December 18, 1986

regulation of financial institutions. One recognizes that, but the reform process started with the previous Government. Departmental officials were at work on it. There were a whole series of internal discussion papers. The former Minister of State for Finance had set up an eminent group of industry and consumer representatives to form an advisory committee.
This Government inherited all that and spoke of bringing in comprehensive legislation almost from day one of its mandate. Despite all the events of the past two years, the only thing the Government has done today is to exchange Green Paper proposals for another set of proposals.
In the past two years, there has been on the one hand great change and upheaval in the financial services industry, but on the other hand the Government has given us halfway measures, ad hoc responses, mismanagement, misinformation, astronomical financial costs and devastating human costs. This Government will be remembered for many years to come as the Government that rushed blindly to bail out an ailing bank, that then swore up and down to ail and sundry that the bank was viable, that six months later presided over the spectacular failure of the bailed out bank and a second bank and that then used taxpayers' money and special legislation to give 100 per cent reimbursement to all the banks' depositors whose holdings exceeded the $60,000 ceiling for deposit insurance.
The numbers are not in yet, but it is no exaggeration to estimate the costs of the bank failures at $2 billion. Two years and $2 billion later, how much further ahead are we in terms of having legislation in place? There are two pieces of legislation on the Order Paper. Today's discussion paper indicates that legislation will be introduced in this Session of Parliament. We do not know how long this Session will last. Perhaps it will last for another two years.
The human costs of the Government's bungling have also been considerable. Canadian Commercial Bank employees, for example, had their lives disrupted and their careers damaged by the bank's failure. I am talking about the bank's junior and middle-management staff, not the high-flyers and senior managers who made the decisions that got the bank into trouble in the first place. I am referring to moderately-paid staff members, people with families who lost their jobs and did not even get the severance benefits to which they were entitled under the Canada Labour Code. Either deliberately or by sloppy procedures this Government arranged matters so as to deprive employees of the severance benefits to which they were entitled by law. There has been a clear violation of the Canada Labour Code. I understand that officials of Labour Canada are now preparing to a lay a claim on behalf of those Canadian Commercial Bank employees.
I might also mention the Canadian Commercial Bank shareholders who relied as much as depositors did on the Government's worthless assurances of the bank's viability, assurances that were made in letters to shareholders less than a month before the bank went into liquidation. Many of those
Statements by Ministers
shareholders were not market speculators but people of modest means who had done their best to make safe and prudent investments to prepare for retirement. They lost everything.
The damage done to confidence in the financial system in the wake of the bank failures resulted in other human tragedies. The British Columbia Teachers Investment and Housing Co-operative, once the largest co-operative in British Columbia, suffered a run on deposits at the time of the CCB bail-out as well as when the CCB closed. As a result, the co-op went into voluntary receivership. Forty-five thousand co-op members, many of them retired teachers, saw their retirement planning thrown completely off course. They had no access to their savings for many months. When a restructuring agreement for the co-op was finally reached they received only 51 per cent of their savings back in cash.
This is a genuinely tragic series of events for thousands of Canadians who had worked and saved for a prudent retirement, and who quite justifiably traced the source of their misfortune to the weakening of confidence that was a byproduct of the Government's bungling of the Canadian Commercial Bank crisis. Still we do not have the comprehensive systematic reform legislation in place to prevent such things from happening again. What we have had is a series of occasions in the House over the past two years when Parliament was forced to consider and approve in great haste legislation to tidy up some of the situations that arose because of the lack of legislation to prevent them.
There was Bill C-50 in respect of the Pioneer Trust Company; there was Bill C-37 to bail out the Canadian Commercial Bank; there was Bill C-79 to bail out the uninsured depositors of the Canadian Commercial and Northland banks, and earlier this month there was Bill C-27 to enable the HongKong Bank to take over the Bank of British Columbia.
In April of this year the Government approved the takeover of a financial institution by a non-financial organization against the recommendation of the Standing Committee on Finance and Economic Affairs. Other financial institutions have closed their doors. Still others were taken over by other institutions both foreign owned and Canadian owned. Still the Government operated in a policy vacuum.
Concern about corporate concentration has grown as financial holding companies and large corporations increase in size and their links with the financial services sector proliferate. Concern about corporate concentration has been raised in the House on more than one occasion by the Leader of the Official Opposition.
At least twice.

It was also raised by the Official Opposition members of the House of Commons Finance Committee in our minority report on the Government's Green Paper. In the last few months prominent industry people have spoken out on the risks and the need for government action.

December 18, 1986
Statements by Ministers
One really must continue to be amazed at why the Government has not acted sooner or more decisively to ensure that the accelerating pace of change in the financial services industry works for Canada and for Canadians.
Recently there was a major Canadian bank that established a securities dealership in the freer market of the Province of Quebec, doing so legally by making ingenious and creative use of an obscure section of the Bank Act. It was obliged to proceed in such a way because federal legislation is so drastically out of step with the realities of today's financial services industry.
Today we have what the Minister calls new directions. Tie talks about a pragmatic approach to ownership. That pragmatic approach might perhaps be more accurately described as a status quo approach. The question of ownership of financial institutions, particularly of ownership of financial institutions by commercial enterprises, is one that many people have been concerned about. But this Government's response is what it calls a pragmatic approach, which translates as complete grandfathering of every situation that now exists where commercial enterprises own financial institutions.
There are vague statements in the proposal before us, such as future acquisitions will have to be approved by the Minister of Finance. There are no criteria. Let us hope that the criteria will be produced and will be in the legislation. Otherwise, if it is left to ministerial discretion, the Government has merely opened the doors wide to a continuation of the type of lobbying that has taken place in recent months where those who have the most access to the Minister's ear get the legislation they want.
It is interesting that in this particular proposal the trust companies are the big winners. Trust companies are about to acquire all the powers of banks without any of the restraints, up until about 1990 or 1991 when there will be some restraints, but none as demanding as those of the banks.
There are some interesting statements here that are not developed. For instance, there are two references in the document to what is going on with our financial services subject to industry, and the possible changes as being "trade negotiations now underway". This Government has never officially said that the financial services industry is part of the bilateral negotiations with the United States, although we have had good reason to think that is the case. Certainly, with the proposals that the Minister has before us, some very important bargaining chips are being given away. There is no indication of what, if anything, has been gained in return.
There is a nod or two in this document to competition. We learn that large financial institutions cannot acquire subsidiaries, that they must create them. "Build not buy" is the slogan used, which is an attractive slogan. Side-by-side with this comes the lack of clarity. We are told that a large institution cannot buy a large institution. What is "large"? Where are the definitions? Side-by-side with this type of statement is the rather loose statement that implies that a Minister can in fact
approve any takeover or acquisition. It may very well be that the legislation will have firmer criteria, but what is before us now is not very reassuring.
There are some positive promises in the document, but again we must wait to see how they will be carried out. There is an indication that co-operative financial institutions may benefit from new legislation. For those of us who are familiar with the co-op movement and think it is a very important citizen and consumer movement, obviously we would be pleased to see some broadening of powers and some additional protection for consumers. However, again we have to wait for the details.
It is interesting that networking is being allowed except for retail insurance. Independent insurance brokers must be complimented on the very effective way in which they flooded Members of Parliament with letters. They certainly got results.
There is a particular statement in the main document that develops a little on the build-not-buy theme which I mentioned earlier. If it had been previously implemented, we would not have had the Bank of British Columbia necessarily going into foreign hands or another bank going into the hands of Lloyd's Bank. If the proposals mentioned in the document had been in place, Canadian institutions would have been able to buy both banks. We have seen two foreign banks obtain a tremendous advantage in terms of being able to buy banks which already had branches and considerable retail banking business. The barn-door has been closed after the Hongkong Bank and Lloyd's Bank have bought here. Though perhaps better late than never, one must point out that it is very late.
There is mention in one of the documents of an attempt to get better harmonization of federal and provincial regulatory policies. Obviously it is a very desirable aim. However, how will it be achieved and when will it be achieved? For those answers we have to wait for the next instalment in the Minister's ongoing saga.
In summary, there is very little to which one could object in the document because it is mostly puffery and mostly statements of good, general principles. There is very little indication of when, if ever, these principles will be adopted. If indeed the legislation comes forward, we will want to see more specifics in it. However, it would be very nice if the Minister could indicate today a firm date for the legislation, rather than sometime next year or sometime before the end of the session.

Mr. Speaker, I have a number of comments on the statement which I have spent some time absorbing in the lock-up? There are some sighs of relief in the corporate boardrooms of the interests which own a large stake of Canada. I suspect as well that there are whoops of joy in certain boardrooms of banks and trust companies as a consequence of the policy announced by the Minister, which in fact represents some substantial changes. I do not necessarily say that I agree with them, but at least there is a policy in
December 18, 1986

place. Had the policy been in place previously, some of the failures, which have seen control of Canadian banks go into foreign hands and more than $1 billion flow out of the pockets of taxpayers and of the Canada Deposit Insurance Company accounts and into the pockets of depositors, would have been prevented. At the same time there is a sense of impending doom or, at the very least, uncertainty in the offices of brokers and investment dealers on Bay Street and on St. James Street, because their comfortable, cosy, walnut panelled world will change very quickly.
This is Canada's answer to the big bang. We could say that the big bang will mean big bucks for certain people. It protects the interests of certain of the big buck artists in Canada, notably the wealthy families who control certain financial holding companies and whose ability to continue their privileged position is affected only minimally. If anything, they are protected from being overtaken from the rear by the proposals in the Minister's statement and, therefore, their ability to make big bucks may in fact improve.
There are new opportunities for financial institutions in the proposals put forward by the Minister and the Government. However, there are not commensurate guarantees of benefits for ordinary Canadians. This is very serious. It is one thing about which we will be talking a fair amount in the new year when the policy statement begins to be translated into actual legislation.
There are questions in terms of where financial services are provided and in terms of the maltreatment and harassment suffered by farmers, small business people, and ordinary income earners perhaps affected unemployment, at the hands of financial institutions. There is not a breath or whisper of a word of any concern in that regard. The Government speaks of a balance in this statement, but it is balance between the differrent interests in the financial industry. It does not speak of a balance to redress the power of small income earners, small business people, farmers, fishermen and such people, against the billion dollar institutions regulated in the particular policy.
The policy speaks of competition which may or may not result. However, it is quite clear that there will be increased concentration, which troubles us a great deal.
When I looked at the statement, I wondered what my Party would be looking for in terms of financial services policy. Clearly there is a need to increase capacity to handle certain levels of financing, for example, and to increase flexibility. However, I would contend that it is not automatic with an accompanying increase in concentration, yet concentration is what is being delivered in the statement.
Finally there is a virtual elimination of the indepedence of investment dealers and brokers. Within a year and a half they will find themselves taken over or forced into alliances with banks, insurance companies, trust companies, or foreign financial institutions. That will happen rapidly. I am concerned about what will be the consequence of taking one of the
Statements by Ministers
four pillars and effectively eliminating it completely, at the same time as the other three are being collapsed together. Far be it from me, a New Democratic or democratic socialist, to leap to the defence of Rosedale, Westmount, and Shaughnessy Heights. Nonetheless, an ironic result of the reform announced by the Government is that the Canadian investment industry, which has served as a somewhat independent source of advice, will now be rolled into banks and other financial institutions.
For example, I refer to an entrepreneur doing business with a bank and being extended a line of credit. The bank may turn around and say I am sorry, your company is getting to the limit of your line of credit. We think you should do an equity issue, and we think you should do it with this company with whom we happen to be related in the investment industry. If the entrepreneur is not so sure about that and thinks about going down the street to another bank, he runs a risk that the line of credit will be threatened by the bank seeking to move business over to its investment subsidiary. That is a very real threat, according to the proposals of the Government.
I feel the Government is adopting the gospel of deregulation from the United States. It is ironic that it is doing so in a week where the prophets of deregulation around Ronald Reagan are pleading the Fifth Amendment, being forced to resign, discredited, or seeking refuge back in Wall Street because they cannot hack it in a political environment. Nonetheless, the true believers still exist here in Canada so that gospel continues to be preached. However, it is done in a way which leads me to question the benefits for ordinary Canadians, be they businessmen, fishermen, farmers or consumers.
At the time of the release of the report of the Standing Committee on Finance and Economic Affairs dealing with financial institutions, the committee took issue in a very major way with the recommendations of the Green Paper of a year or so ago. In our minority report we focused on the issue of the concentration of financial power in the Canadian financial services industry, and in industry generally. We urged tough restrictions on ownership and that ownership rules be extended to trust companies and other financial institutions. We suggested the 10 per cent rule should be extended to trust companies and financial institutions.
What is significant is that in the wake of the Imasco takeover of Canada Trust in April of 1986, the committee as a whole moved a very long way in the same direction as suggested by our minority report in January or February of this year. The committee recommended that a non-financial corporation should only be able to own 30 per cent. It also suggested retroactivity. That is, there should not be a grandfathering of the current situation where major trust companies are controlled by non-financial companies. This has created a concentration of economic and financial power which both I and my party believe poses grave risks to Canada's economic development and the proper working of the market system.

December 18, 1986
Statements by Ministers
When the Government came to consider that issue this fall we found it was not a serious issue with the Government at all. It casually allowed a couple of banks, the Continental and the Bank of British Columbia, to sell out to foreign banks because it was more profitable for shareholders than keeping them in Canadian hands. The Government looked at the recommendations, and then I guess what happened was that the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney), the President of the Treasury Board (Mr. de Cotret), the former Minister of State for Finance, and two or three others started to press the Government to prevent that recommendation of the committee being adopted. The Minister of State for Finance (Mr. Hockin) is shaking his head. This has been widely reported and if he wants to deny it, that is fine. I think a lot of people are convinced that is the case.
One thing which I think is significant in the proposals is that, in future, acquisitions of one financial corporation by another will be subjected to ministerial approval. When we were in the lock-up, officials from the Department of Finance did not blink an eye when it was suggested that that might mean it is okay for one $10 billion financial institution to take over another $10 billion financial institution and create an institution with $20 billion in assets, but that if perhaps a big bank were to take over an institution with $5 billion in assets that might not be acceptable. In other words, it is not a matter of tiny trust companies with $500 million in assets-which does not sound that tiny but in general it is small-being taken over, but that major mergers are contemplated as being acceptable to the Minister under this policy.
We all know that Ministers of Finance are politicians. They come from the party in power and are subject to influence, among other things, by corporations which are close to the party in power. It is very interesting that instead of getting a 30 per cent rule we got a 65 per cent rule. The Government says that if a commercial corporation has control of a financial institution it will have to reduce its ownership from the current level to no more than 65 per cent. That is still control in any language. If I had 65 per cent of the vote in my riding I would be extremely happy. In addition, the 65 per cent is held to. As the company requires more equity, it will be allowed to continue at the 65 per cent level.
I grant you that having a widely held 35 per cent will require a certain window on those particular companies which does not exist right now. There is some improvement and not everything is to be criticized in the proposal. Nonetheless, why a 65 per cent rule instead of 30 per cent? Is it because, for example, the Brascan group, controlled by Peter and Edward Bronfman, which in turn controls Trilon Financial, which in turn controls both Royal Trust and London Life, contributed $15,000 to the Progressive Conservative Party?
Oh, oh!
I think that must have been in 1984. Royal Trust put $13,000 into the hands of the Conservative Party. London Life contributed $6,353.
Order!

It is therefore open, with this ministerial discretion on acquisitions and takeovers, to companies to decide it is good business to put tens of thousands of dollars into the hands of the party in power in order to get a favourable reception and get the Minister's ear. Imasco is very much involved because they seek grandfathering of their takeover of Canada Trust. That trust company gave $8,000 to the Conservative Party in 1984 or 1985. The Minister winces but that is what they gave.
I am not wincing.

Imasco gave $36,594. Again, is that why they are being allowed to continue with 65 per cent ownership of a multibillion dollar trust company at a time when no new commercial interests will be allowed to do the same thing? What about Power Corp? That is another good friend of Governments in power on both sides, that is Liberals and Conservatives. Great West Life gave $10,000. That is a subsidiary of Power Corp. Montreal Trust gave $36,657.

Point of order, Mr. Speaker. As far as I recall there are rules of this Chamber which deal with imputing motives to Ministers when they make policy. The insinuations we are hearing now, that policy changes were made and legislation proposed on the basis of amounts of money which might have been made as donations to a political party, are not acceptable.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: I do not find that to be a point of order.

Mr. Speaker, I am honoured to be in agreement with your very sound and sage opinion. I think government Members are perhaps a bit sensitive. I am simply recording facts and asking a question which I think many ordinary Canadians ask. They wonder whether their interests are being respected when large corporations are being allowed to concentrate financial power, despite the fact that there are some desirable reforms put forward by the Government in today's statement.
Tell us who else they gave money to.
The Hon. Member makes a comment. Perhaps he can make it again because I did not quite catch it.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Communications; Deputy Whip of the Progressive Conservative Party
speechtext: You know very well he cannot because he cannot speak.

In that case perhaps he should allow me to make my comments on the statement by the Minister.
The standing committee unanimously recommended a 30 per cent limit on ownership and we did not get it. The committee was looking for a real curb on concentration of financial power and we did not get it. The committee delivered a
December 18, 1986

carefully considered report and it was ignored by the Government. Instead, the Government has only limited future intrusion by commercial groups into the financial sector, which means that the privileged position of Brascan, Power Corporation, Imasco and such corporations is, if anything, more valuable than if the Government had applied the same rules to everyone. They need only divest by 35 per cent in 1991. They can do that by simply inviting the public to share for a while in the ownership without, at the same time, reducing their stake in these corporations.
New opportunities are being given to financial institutions, including the trust companies. The powers which trust companies will enjoy will make them like banks in almost everything but name. Yet, the Government ignored the very sensible proposals of the Economic Council of Canada that companies engaged in banking, whether provincially or federally regulated, should be regulated as banks because of the federal power in the BNA Act with regard to banking. If anything, the trust companies are on more than an equal footing. Once their assets exceed $500 million, they will now enjoy unrestricted commercial lending instead of labouring under a 7 or 10 per cent restriction as they do now. They will have unrestricted access to consumer loans. They will be able to enter the securities business and do everything except call themselves banks.
Deregulation is no guarantee that there will be safeguards for ordinary consumers. The Government speaks of a reorganization of the Office of the Inspector General of Banks with the Department of Insurance. It has been decided not to roll the Canada Deposit Insurance Corporation into that because they want to have separation, for reasons I am not entirely clear on. The intention is then to create a committee which will be composed of the Superintendent of Financial Insitutions, the Deputy Minister of Finance, the Governor of the Bank of Canada and the President of the Canada Deposit Insurance Corporation. Their job will be to avoid trouble.
There is a real problem with regard to the adequacy of regulation whether or not these two offices are rolled into one. I would like to remind my friend, the Minister, that the Governor of the Bank, the Deputy Minister of Finance, the Inspector General of Banks and the President of the CDIC sat together on the board of the Canada Deposit Insurance Corporation during the time that the people of Canada saw $1.25 billion go down the drain due to mistakes in the regulation and operation of some banks. If they could not get it together when they were meeting on the board of the CDIC, one wonders whether they will be able to get it together in this forum unless there is a very strong commitment to more adequate regulation.
We will be raising this during the course of discussion on the forthcoming Bill. I hope the Minister will take that stand. I hope he realizes, among other things, that we will have to have the resources which the former Inspector General, Mr. Statements by Ministers
Kennet, argued for, but did not have the gumption to resign over when he became aware several years ago that the IGB's office was inadequately equipped to do its job.
I spoke earlier about ordinary Canadians.

For instance, I might mention the owner of a business in Chicoutimi, a farmer in Alberta's Peace River region, a man who has a store in Happy Valley in Labrador, or a young family in Le Pas, Manitoba. Do these people have a guarantee that services will improve, that competition will better serve their interests, or perhaps are they going to pay higher prices while at the same time the institutions they deal with will be doing much better business in places like Montreal, Toronto and Vancouver?
That is a real problem, Mr. Speaker. We might find ourselves in a situation where this financial supermarket will be created for wealthier middle and upper income Canadians, people who earn really good money, but then ordinary people will not be able to benefit from it.

They may even have to pay $10 for a bounced cheque because the bank is trying to increase its revenues because it made some bad loans in Latin America, or because it bought a securities company and, as in London, paid fancy salaries to some of the people it brought on board and then found out it was not making a profit.
There are real problems with regard to the failure of the Government to address the need to protect services and ensure adequate, affordable services for ordinary Canadians. We must ensure that young entrepreneurs are not forced out of business because they cannot get an extra loan to help build up the business. We must ensure that farmers are not forced out of business because the loans which were forced upon them three years ago are now being called, as has happened in too many instances. We must ensure that farmers do not have to fight back with a penny auction because of the regressive attitude of the banks and the way in which they are trying to victimize their former customers.
With regard to foreign ownership, we are concerned that since foreign owners will be treated as domestic, they will be given unlimited power to acquire securities companies after a brief delay of a year and a half, and, after that, any other financial corporation. We are concerned that the restrictions on nonresidents only apply to the very large institutions. I mentioned the concern about Bay Street and St. James Street. I do not suggest that our voters are there, but to alienate that entire sector raises questions in my mind.
I would like to speak positively to the Minister about the fact that the Government listened to the concerns of people in the life insurance business. A lot of small agents raised their concerns through Members on all sides of the House. The Government has responded by excluding from networking the

December 18, 1986

power to sell life and casualty insurance over the counter in these financial supermarkets. That is welcome.
We are concerned about the rather curious situation wherein a commercial interest cannot enter into the trust or loan company business but can buy into such a business if the Minister permits. There seems to be some contradiction there which we will have to explore when this matter comes before committee.
Finally, I would like to say a word-
That's the fourth "finally".

I have the right to speak for as long as the Minister did. I will speak for only that long. If the Hon. Member for Western Arctic (Mr. Nickerson) does not like what a real socialist has to say in the House of Commons, we will take his seat in the next election and his constituents will have a New Democrat to represent them. If he does not want to listen to me now, he can take his absence and go off to a Christmas party. I wish his constituents a merry Christmas and a happy new year.
With regard to the way in which these institutions work, we should not think only of the market and of modeling ourselves after what is happening in London, Germany, or the United States. We must also consider our needs here. For example, I would like a requirement that in every region where a financial institution oeprates there be an advisory committee made up of consumers, small business people, and perhaps people from municipal government, who provide input to that institution and seek to ensure that that institution really serves the needs of that area. I would like to ensure that a searchlight could be shone upon situations which we discover, such as that which existed in the Bank of British Columbia.
In the last three or four years chartered bank deposits in British Columbia have increased by approximately $10 billion, but the money has not been invested in British Columbia. Unemployment has been soaring in that province and the money saved by British Columbians was invested in central Canada. There is something fundamentally wrong with that.
I would like the consumers and clients of the banks and financial institutions to be guaranteed a voice on the board of directors of those financial institutions. Rather than requiring that a limited number of directors, who would be largely of like mind with the internal directors, sit on the boards of these
corporations, we should ensure that ordinary Canadians have a voice in and a window on what happens in those institutions.
From time to time my Party speaks about the need to democratize these centres of power and put them in the hands of ordinary Canadians. I suggest that those are some constructive and positive means by which we could seek to do that.
Over the Christmas break, a time of peace and goodwill to people here in Canada and around the world, I hope the Minister of State for Finance and his colleagues could incorporate some of those suggestions in their proposals as they turn them into legislation to be considered by the House in the new year.
In closing, I want to wish the Minister of State for Finance and his colleagues a Merry Christmas and Happy New Year. I know that we will be very intensively involved with these proposals for many months in the new year.
This may have been said earlier, but I think all Hon. Members would want to join me in expressing our good wishes to one of my colleagues from the National Capital Region, the Hon. Member for Gatineau (Mrs. Mailly), who is going to be wed on December 23.1 know every Member of Parliament will wish her and her spouse the best.
Hear, hear!
